summary: The assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31. 1965 and March 31., 1967 respectively. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,04,636/ in the net wealth of the assessee on the basis of cash system of accounting. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system, the accrued interest on the money lending investments could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Assistant commissioner followed "Commissioner of Wealth Tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth Tax officer appealed to this Court. Dismissing the reference, ^ HELD: 1.1 In order to determine the assets of an assessee, it is necessary that the valuation date for the purposes of this Act should be the last day of the previous year as defined in section 3 of the Income Tax Act. [309E] 1.2 The method of accounting, mercantile or cash or hybrid, is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of the assesse are maintained on cash basis interest due on accrual basis, though not realised, on the outstandings of the money lent business are liable to be included In the net Wealth of the appellant. [310F] 1:3 The method adopted by the assessee in determining the value date in terms of the last date of the income tax "previous year" stop there. The system of valuation, mercantile, or cash, is a principle evolved by courts and tribunals. It is not necessary that each asset must be considered as an asset other than cash, its value being determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Wealth tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation dates. [334G H; 310A] 1 :4 The method for determining the net assets of the assesses is not arbitrary or fanciful but a device to avoid evasion of tax. It has been held by this Court in Commissioner of Wealth tax vs Vickayaraju B Cadreenarayana Murthy, ; , that the method adopted in determining its assets and debts as on the value dates is not unreasonable. [311C] 1;5 The method followed by the Income tax Officer in determining his net wealth is not reasonable. It does not mean that the asset should be considered to have been used for a purpose other than the one which was intended to be achieved by the statute. [313E F] 2.1 The method prescribed by the Wealthtax Act, as the valuation day, under the Wealth (Tax) Act, is not discriminatory or arbitrary. It cannot be said that the methods adopted in fixing the net asset are unreasonable. It would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [328G H] 2:2 In order that a particular method may be adopted for determining assets of a assessee under the wealth Tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net income of the deceased on the Valuation date. The valuation date is not fixed by any consideration of the particular system of accountancy adopted by him. [330F] 2 :3 In order, therefore, the inference is inescapable, that even if the accounts are maintained at cash basis, interest due thereon would fetch If sold in open market, on valuation date, though no realised, the value is determined pursuant thereto sub section(I) as the estimate price which, according to the WealthTax Officer, is determined upon pursuant to subsection (I).

The respondent was a workman of the Central Administrative Tribunal. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been convicted on a criminal charge. The appel lant challenged his dismissal before the Central Adminis tration Tribunal, which held that the penalty imposed by the disciplinary authority was not justified and ordered his reinstatement in service with back wages. The Tribunal also directed that the respondent should be reinstated in service forthwith. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel tant that the order imposing a lesser penalty on the respond ents could not be supported on any finding as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment could lawfully be imposed, it was not for the. Respondent contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction if the findings of the Enquiry Officer or the Tribunal prima facie make out a case of misdemeanour and to direct the authority to reconsider the penalty, for as he had ma de his choice of forum and was even otherwise dealt with und er the Government Servants (Conduct) Rules which are undispu tedly applicable to him. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order imposing the lesser penalty cannot be sustained. [33E] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had ma re de his choices of forum, and was therefore even otherwise deal ing with undi t he Government Servants ' (Conduct ) Rules which were undispu stedly available to him, is n ot justifiable. [34F G] 1:3 The Tribunal could not interfere with the penalty if the conclusion of the enquiry officer or the competent authority is based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. This power has been conceded to the cou rt in Union of India vs Tulsiram Patel, ; , referred to. [35F] 1 :4 The Tribunal can interfere with penalty if t he conclusion of th e enquiry officer and the competent authori ty is based upon evidence even though some of them are found to have been irrelevant or irrelevant to the matters. This jurisdiction has been expressly conceded to by the Supreme Court in Union Of India vs Hari Shankar Das, ; ; , relied on. [36F] 2.1 In the light of the principles to which we have call ed attention and in view of the aforesaid discussion, the ord er of the Tribunal imposing a higher penalty on t he respond ent cannot, therefore, be sustained.[37A] 1.:4. The order of the High Court imposing a lower penalty on th e respond ent is set aside.

The appellants were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff Inacio Martins who died pendente lite. He had filed a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 1. The first ground on which the High Court dismissed the suit was that the suit had been barred by the principle of res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 157 of 1968 and hence, the subsequent suit was based on a distinct cause of action not found in the former case and hence the bar of Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The second suit based on the factum of tenancy was dismissed as the Trial Court came to the conclusion that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the property in respect of which he claimed to be a lessee. It would have been a different matter if in the previous suit the court had decided the question of status as lessee against the plaintiff, in which case, perhaps it could be argued that the second suit founded on the facts of the earlier suit was not maintainable. The High Court took the view that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of his land within the period allowed by Section 18 of the Act and had, therefore, allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the suit property on the strength of his tenancy. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question which arose in the suit is whether defendant No 1 was a tenant or a deemed tenant. [1032C] 1.2 In such a situation the remedy may not be the one available in the case of a tenant other than a deemed tenants whose case is not governed by section 8(2) of Act. But in the cases of a deemed lessee who has been evicted from the land on or after 1st July, 1962 since a remedy has been provided under 1032 the Act, the Jurisdiction of the Civil Courts stands wholly barred by virtue of Section 58 (2) read section 58(2). [1033D] 2.1 In such an event the remedy would not be one available to the Civil Court to give any relief to the landlord by way of possession of agricultural land. If, on the other hand, the Mamlatdar rejects the plea raised under the Tenancy Act, he would be entitled to deal with the dispute on the footing that the defendant is a trespasser. [ 1034E] 2:2 In the instant case, the suit in question was based upon a distinct and cause of actions not found against the appellant. The jurisdiction of the civil court stands wholly excluded by virtue Section 58(1) of Bombay Tenancy Act. Therefore, the question which arises in the present suit was whether defendant 1 was tenant or deemed tenant was required to be decided by the Mamlatdar under section 7 read section 8 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. [1004G] 2 :3 In such circumstances, the Civil court would not have been competent to pass any order for restoration of possession to the deemed tenant, because it would not otherwise be open to the civil Court to grant any relief in favour of the landlord.

The petitioners are carpenters. They demand payment in terms paid to their counterparts in regular services. The Corporation has clearly stated that there were no regular employees of the petitioners ' categories in its establishment and, as such, the question of payment to the petitioners does not arise. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that the Corporation has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. The financial aspect of the Corporation is stated to be not encouraging, and indeed it is disappointing. But To avoid or minimizing further loss it is submitted that the Court has pointed out that there are bumper cases filed in this Court for enforcement of the right to equality before the law and also to seek relief from the State. The Court, therefore, cannot direct the Corporation to apply the rates prescribed under exhibit P. 2 unless the Government makes it applicable to employees of Government service. [669G H] Randhir Singh vs Union of India & Ors., ; ; ; Randhir Singh case, ; ; State of Punjab vs Randhir Singh, ; , State of Haryana vs Randhir singh, ; and State of U.P. vs RandhirSingh, ; referred to. The principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. There can be no quarrel with the proposition that equal pay for Equal work is a concomitant of Article 14 of the Constitution. But equal pay must depend upon the nature of the work done, it cannot be judged by the mere volume of work, there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. It is important to emphasize that equal work for equal Work is a component of Article14 of the constitution. From the averments in the pleadings of the parties it will be clear that the petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the . By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter or craftsman is equal to the other in the performance of his work. The principal claim of the peti tioners therefore fails and is rejected.

The prosecution case was that on the date of occurrence, the deceased and his wife were staying in a house at about 9.30 p.m. The accused 1 to 3 were armed with deadly weapons and they were armed by their side. They were armed and were armed. On seeing them, the accused persons ran away from the place of occurrence. The deceased was taken to the hospital where he died on the way. The prosecution case further alleged that the accused had assaulted his wife and daughter in a car. The trial court convicted all the seven accused under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life under section 304 Part II read with Section 34 I P.C., and also to pay fine of Rs. 500/ each, and in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded to accused 1 and 6 for the murder of Malan. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against him in view of the fact that he had been acquitted by the High Court of the charge of conspiracy under section 120B I. P. C.; (2) the confessional statement of accused 6 could not have been relied upon as a substantive piece of evidence; and (3) the confession of the accused 5 was inadmissible in evidence because it was retracted from his earlier statement recorded under section 164 Cr. P., which was not admissible in evidence. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confessions of accused 4 could not therefore be relied on against accused 6 in view Of the fact, that accused 6 had been convicted by the trial court and sentenced to imprisonment for death under section 306 read with s 34 IP. C., and the confirmation of the conviction of accused 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 by the Sessions Judge under section302 read with S 34 I I.A. could be sustained. [138 F] 2. The confession of Accused 6 was admissible in the trial proceedings as it was not retracted from the earlier statement made to him under section164 Cr.P., which had been recorded under Section 164 Cr P. P, and therefore, the retracted confession of an accused 5 cannot be relied against him. [139 G H] 3. The confessional statement made by accused 6 was inadmissible because it did not contain a recital that the deceased was in any way responsible for the commission of the offence. [140 C D] 4. The confessions of the two accused were admissible in law and could not, therefore, be relied only against accused 1, 6 and 7. [141 E F] 5. The statement made before the police under section 161 Cr. A. No. 348/79 was inadmissible as evidence because the confession was retracted by the accused.

The appellant 's father had executed a will in favour of the respondent, and so Lakshmamma was not competent to make a will. The appellant ' s son died on August 22, 1945, leaving behind his widow, two daughters and one daughter. The respondent filed a suit for possession of certain properties. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the will in question was not proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmma. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the testatrix had no clear recollection as to what happened on the day when she attested the will, and that the evidence adduced by the appellant was highly improbable; and that even if it had found in favour Of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that the testator fully understood the nature and effect of the dispositions before she put her signature to the will. Held, that the High court was in error in coming to the conclusion that it was not shown that the propounder fully understood its contents. The evidence of the attesting witness was clearly inconsistent with the appellant ' 's case about previous instructions and so it would be necessary to refer to the broad features, and dispositions of the will and the evidence led by the respondent to prove its execution. The onus was heavy on him to remove the suspicions attending the execution of the document and to establish that Lakshmabai had really understood its terms and put her signatures to the document of his own free will.

The appellant company, a manufacturer of Arc carbons manufactured by the respondent company, was assessed to sales tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fall under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act '). The appellant company filed an application before the Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P., claiming that they fell under entry 41 of the Schedule to the Act and claimed exemption from sales tax on the grounds that they were falling under entry Nos. 4 and 5 of the said Schedule. The Assistant Commissioner allowed the application holding that the goods fell under item No.4 of the schedule to the Andhra State General Sales tax Act, 1956 (hereinafter called 'the Andhra Pradesh Act ') and that they did not fall under Entry 41 of Schedule 1 of the Act. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal which held that the entry in the Schedule was "accessories" within the meaning of entry No, 4 of Schedule I of the Madras General Salestax Act, 1958 (hereinafter to be referred to hereinafter as 'The Act '), and that the sales tax authorities were compelled to consider the use which is generally made of the arc carbon. The Tribunal held that these are carbers falling under item 41 of schedule 1 of Andhra Pradesh State General sales Tax Act 1957, and that in both cases what was decided was whether "welding electrodes", considered by themselves, were "electrical goods" falling within entry 41 Of Schedule I to the Mysore Sales Tax Rules, 1957. The High Court also held that such arc car bons under consideration fall within the relevant entry 4 of schedule I of Andhra State Act and that, therefore, they fell within the entry No., 4 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to that Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the High Court had erred in holding that these arc carcons were covered by the entry under consideration. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that "accessory" is used in the schedule and describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. It will be noticed that the word "accessary" is generally used in several entries, such as entry No,. Of course, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for using a particular kind of instrument of gadget only, the article manufactured to serve as a part of a particular type of apparatus would not cease to be covered by that intended entry merely because a purchaser makes some other use of it. [601 B C] 2. The word " Accessories" is employed in several Entries, such like entry Nos. Of course even where the entry relates for parts manufactured or for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment. It would be noticed from the fact that they are known as "cinema arc carboons". [602 D] 3. The term "accessaries" is not used in any of the entries, but in the context in which it occurs. The entry No 4 occurs in a schedule in which descriptions of goods to be taxed indicate that the expression "required for use there with" has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. It may be satisfactorily determined in the light of the language of the entry itself considered in the background in which the it occurs, [603 E F] 4. The words "parts thereof" are used in various entries,such as entry Nos., Of course , Entry No.

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners contended that the royalty levied and covered under the rules should be applied only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. [419D] 1.2 The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used only for development of minerals and not for other purposes sanctioned by law. [416E] 1:3 The Act was passed for decal opment and development of minor minerals, and for purposes connected there with. Rule 18 of the Rules provides for the determination of the rate of royalty payable in respect of minor mineral. The original rule 21 was substituted by new rule 21 by the issue of impugned notification on 26 6 1985 which provided that a holder of a Parwana granted under the Rules shall pay royalty at the rate prescribed for the time being in the rules framed by the State Government in respect o minor minerals except in the case of specified minor mineral and 20 hec tares in the cases of ordinary sand, Kankar Murram Gravel and in the ease of ordinary Sand, Kikar Murram and gravel a lease can be granted upto three years, and the area or land covered by a mining lease is governed by rule 15 which says that no quarry lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case of any specified minor minerals. So a comparison of the relevant rules would show that a larger restriction was imposed both on the area in respect to which a Parna could be issued and the duration of the Parwana right and as also stated that the persons who take quarrying Parwana are persons belonging to the weaker sections of society and if under rule 21 a concession is shown in their favour it cannot be said that there is no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21 to show concession in the matter of payment of royalty and the social policy underlying the Constitution, the statute and the Rules. [414G H; 414A B] 1 :4 The fact that section 15 of the Act does not authorise the State Govern ment to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence. No express power need to conferred on such subordinate authority in order to make a classification for purpose of implementing the policy of the statute under which the Rules are made. [413C D] 1.:5 The fact, that section 17 of the Gujarat Mineral Rules, 1966 does not authorize the State Govt. to show any such concession when promulgating rules which are inconsistent with the provisions of Article 301 of the Constitu tion regarding movement of goods from one State to another for the activity of quarrying do not involve any movement as such. [ 413D] 2.1 In order to achieve this object, the Legislature has enacted the Gujarat minor Mineral Rules 1967. Rule 21 of the rules provides that a person who takes mining lease or any other mineral conces sion granted under any rule made under sub section (1) shall pay royalties at the rates specified in column 1 of the schedule, removed or consumed by him or by his agent, manager, employee, contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the Rate prescribed for that purpose. Rule 19 provides for determination of royalty in respect Of minor minerals and for matters connected therewith.

The appellant was a hereditary trustee of the temple. He took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the Kumaran Koil was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was not a hereditary tenant within the meaning of section 6(9) of Madras Act 19 of 1951. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge Nagapattinam. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the succession was "regulated by usage" and that according to the usage of the Temple the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meeting of the members of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the ambit of section 4(9). HELD: (i) The word "succession" in section 6 (9) is identical in both the Acts. [446 B] (ii) It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is an vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. [427 C D] (iii) The definition of hereditary trustee in section 2(9)(a) of the Act would include even such cases. But the election to the office of trustee in the present case is for a fixed period of two years and not for life. It is, therefore, difficult to hold that there was a succession within As office. [544 E F] (iv) The appellant 's contention that the trusteeship was "occupied by hereditary right or because succession to that office is by nomination by the holder in office" is not correct.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the second accused, Jabamani Nadar alias Kanyakumari Comrade alias Ramu and Thamizharasan in the case of murder of Viswanatham. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the evidence of PW 4 who was afflicted with the fell disease of leprosy; (2) the High Court erred in convicting the second respondent on the sole testimony of PW4 "corroborated by the contents of exhibit P1 (FIR). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The testimony of this solitary eye witness is not reliable and his evidence cannot be rejected with reference to the testimony of a single witness. [707B] 2. The evidence of the sole witness has been rejected with regard to seeing the accused running away from the place where he was sleeping to the place of occurrence. It is also conceivable that those persons, who gathered would not ask PW 4, who arrived at the place a little later, for information with regard regarding the assailants. There is considerable doubt as to this testimony with regard regard to see seeing the appellant running away after the assault is true. [807C D] 3. The fact that the witness has stated in the first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran as his assailant, does not mean that he would not mention about this fact in the second information report. It also stands to reason that those witnesses who gathered at the scene of occurrence a little earlier than PW 4 did not see the assailants who might have had escaped.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of one Amarchand N. Shroff deceased. The Income tax Officer found that the amounts received by the heirs, legal representatives after his death should be deemed to have been received by him if death had not taken place. The Commissioner of Income tax assessed the total income of the deceased person as if the legal representatives were the assessees and the amount was liable to tax under section 24B(1) read with section 24 B (2). In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that on a correct interpretation of section 24A the amounts which were received by Amarchand after his demise should be treated as income received by them if death took place. On reference, the High Court answered in favour of the respondents and against the Commissioner of Incometax. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three subsections of section24B and cannot be extended further than the liability for the income received in the previous year. [707 B] (ii) Where a person dies before the publication of the notice referred to in sub section (1) of section 22 or before he was served with a notice under sub section(2) of Section 34, as the case may be, his executor, administrator or other legal representative shall, on the serving of the notices under sub sections (2) and (3), comply therewith and the Income tax officer may proceed to assess the totalincome of the person as If such executor, ad ministration or other Legal representative were the assessee. [807 C] (iii) The words "any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" mean that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received by his heirs and death, they are liable to be taxed as income (1 ) [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, referred to.

The petitioners who were members of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959, applied for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to make appointments on the posts reserved under the Andhra State Public Employment(Requiresment as specified in the Schedule to the Constitution. The petitioners contended that article 16(3) of the Constitution was ultra vires the Constitution and that the provisions of article 16 were unconstitutional. Held, that the power conferred by article 16 is not absolute but is subject to the limitations imposed by articles 14 and 15 of the constitution. It is a well settled principle of interpretation that where there is no express provision in the Constitution for prescribing any requirement as to residence within the State or Union territory prior to appointment, it is open to Parliament to make any law which prescribes such requirement. The words 'any requirement ' and contends that the requirement may be also as to resident in the State and, therefore, Parliament was competent to enact a law in a special case prescribing requirement as residence in a part of a State. If it chose to speak of residence in parts of State such as Districts, talauqas, cities towns etc., more appropriate and specific language could have been used such as 'any requirements as to residential qualification and it is impossible to think that the Constituent Assembly was thinking of residence within Districts, Taluqas, towns or villages. It follows therefore that section 3 of the Public Employment Act, 1957 in so far as it relates to Telengana (and we say nothing about the other parts) and Rule 3 of Rules under it are ultra vires.

The appellant was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them, also for offences punishable under sections 467 and 471 of the Penal Code. The Additional Sessions judge convicted him on the ground that he had secreted the letter just because it was found in the almirah which was produced by the appellant 's father. He further held that the articles were in his exclusive possession and that being a question to be decided only by the Court of fact, this Court would not re examine the evidence for satisfying itself as to the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions reached by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives jointly with his father and of which the key was furnished by the father; (2) for an officer of the post office to be found guilty for any of the acts specified in section 52 it had further to be shown that he was entrusted with the postal article with respect to which he is alleged to have committed any of those acts. HELD: (1)(a) The prosecution has failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the accused. No presumption can, therefore, be drawn against him that he has secreted them from the mere fact that they were found in his almirah which, at best, may be regarded as being in the joint possession of himself and his father because he had the opportunity to get at the articles and then infer that he must have utilized the opportunity and was therefore in their exclusive possession would be arguing in a circle. [446C D] (b) The High Court could not have held that though the locked almirah contained some large number of articles belonging to the father and since he had an opportunity to procure the articles it could have been established by showing that he is in their joint possession along with his mother because he has the opportunity of getting at the article and then inferred that he should have utilized this opportunity and he was therefore, in their absolute possession would not be arguing for the first time in an appeal under article 136 of the Constitution. [413D] (c) The fact that an officer had in the course of his duties access to postal articles kept or lying in the post Office, the legislature has deliberately enlarged the scope of section 52 so as to encompass secretion, destruction or throwing away of postal articles by an officer even though they may not have been entrusted to him or even though the are riot articles with which he was required or is competent to deal in the way of his duty. [414E] (d) The mere fact of entrustment of the articles by the accused from the post offices (if that is how he came by the articles) would be theft but it has not been found that he committed any theft. It has not, therefore been established that these articles were either in their own possession or jointly with their father because they had the key with him and it must be held that he did not have secreted those articles. [416G H] (e) The evidence of the prosecution is that these documents were found to be in an almirah of the house at which the accused lives jointly alongwith his father. It was, therefore. necessary for the prosecution to prove this fact.

The appellants were convicted of contempt of court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ and further ordered that in case of default they shall undergo simple imprisonment for two weeks. The High Court held that the Nyaya Panchayat had no jurisdiction to pass an order staying proceedings pending before the Nyaya panchayat. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that the Magistrate had no authority to decide the question whether the Nyaya Panchayats exercised judicial powers and, even if the Panch failed to do so, he could not be said to have committed contempt of Court. HELD : (i) The order sheet dated December 25, 1963 was an affidavit filed by the Sarpanch before a person authorised to administer oaths is not bound to do it and, therefore, the Nyaya panchayats exercised judicial power and even if they failed to comply with the directions given by the High court, they could not have proceeded further. [119 D E] (ii) The High Courts did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Panchas was in fact an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised under section 12 of the Act can be said that he has committed contempt. [120 G H] (iii) The Magistrate had not taken cognizance of the application and the affidavit of Mahabir was not a certified copy of the order. [121 C D] (iv) The provisions of section 12(1)(a) of the , are mandatory in character, and they cannot be ignored merely because the Sarpanch had admitted in his deposition that he had to authority to tell Mahabir that his affidavit was not proper.

The appellant was charged with the murder of Sheo Sahai. The Sessions Judge acquitted him on the ground that it was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the appellant made to a Police Officer and that the evidence about the purchase of the sword sufficient to confirm the appellant 's conviction and sentence were insufficient to establish that it must be the appellant who committed the murder. The High Court, however, acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the entire report dictated by the accused was inadmissible as its content amounted to an confession of a particular offence by a person made to another Police Officer; and that in any case the evidence relied upon by the High Court was insufficient to prove that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai, and that he had been falsely accused of the offences. Held: (i) The statement of the extra judicial confession of an accused is supported by the circumstantial evidence and must be accepted as true. The extra judicial confessions of the accused are not admissible in evidence unless they are corroborated by independent evidence with respect to the four matters mentioned in the report and relied on by the courts below. The statements made by the appellants in their police statement regarding the appellant having enmity with Sheo Sahai were inadmissible in law as it was not necessary for the prosecution to prove conclusively that the person who had committed the offence was guilty of murder. The appellants were elected as members of the Madhya Pradesh Munici 493 pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls) Rules 1963. The election was challenged by some of the petitioners on various grounds including that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules notifying that claims and objections should be preferred within a period of 20 days from the date of publication of the said notice before Shri K. S. Sharma, Deputy Collector without following the procedure prescribed for the purpose. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the election process was vitiated on the ground of non compliance with Rule 4 (3) of Madhya Pradesh Pradesh M�unici 49 pal Corporation Act, 1951 and that the declaration of results of all the 44 successful candidates was liable to be quashed. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the petitioners were entitled to issue of the writ prayed for as of right and the delay in filing the petition should have been ignored. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The writ petition itself was presented on December 28, 1978. No satisfactory explanation was given in the course of the petition by the petitioners as to why they delayed the filing of the Petition till December 28. 1978 even though they knew that there was an error in the notices issued under rule 4(2) of Rules notifying the election and also called upon interested persons to prefer claims or objections thereto within a stipulated period. [417C D] 2. The Deputy Collector had asked petitioner No. 1 to file his claim and/or objection within a specified period. It was notified that the nominations could be filed on and after November 25, 1978 and the poll, if necessary, would take place on December 31, 1978, in all the 43 constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants herein presented a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh Kumar Mishra vs State of M.P., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 829 and 16/79. The final publication of these electoral roll under Rule 8 was done on November 25. 1978. Thereafter the calendar of events was published on November 28, 1979 notifying that the poll if necessary would take places on December 30, 1978 in all 44 constituencies: six petitioners including petitioner No., They further pleaded that the authorities would have taken action to correct the error in notice issued Under Rule 4 of the rules prescribing that claims or objection should be made within a prescribed period. The petitioners were not entitled to the issue of such writ prayed as of rights and the delays in filing their petition should be ignored. [409D E] 3. The contention that the Collector had been informed about the defect was rightly rejected by the High court as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay. [413E F] 4. The question whether the petitioners are entitled to a relief of right or the delay is one of fact and not of law. It is difficult to place any reliance on the said news item for the purposes of concluding that the District Magistrate had been intimated about the defects in the Notice issued under Rules 4(3) and (1). [413C D; 413A] 5. The Collector, Raipur had been apprised about the fact that there were an error apparent on the face of the record. He had asked petitioners No. 2 to file their claims and/ or objections within a particular period. No satisfactorily explanation was furnished in the petition as to how they delayed filing of petitions till December 31.

The respondent company was incorporated in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The company was formed under the Companies Act, 1956 and it was registered as a limited company under the Indian Companies Act. It was registered with the Registrar of Companies Act on December 3, 1967. The Company was incorporated under the provisions of the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1968. The respondent company had been carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The appellant company was also incorporated under section 2(g) of the , and it had been registered as an Indian company under section 5 of the . The company had its office at Hyderabad. It had been maintaining a large number of offices in the said place. The members of the company were also carrying on various activities. The companies were also incorporated in India. The shares of the respondent company were transferred to and vested in the appellant company. The share capital of the Company was Rs. 1,50,000 each. The balance sheet and profit and loss account of the appellant as required under section 220(1) of that Act were submitted by the respondent to the Registrar on or before 30 10 1967. On or before December 31, 1967 the Registrar issued a notice to the company calling upon it to show cause why the balance sheet should not be kept in abeyance for a period of one month from the date of receipt of the notice. The notice was served on the company on January 3, 1968 and the appellant filed its reply on February 4, 1968 denying the allegations made against it. The Registrar of companies issued a show cause notice to it on March 31, 1968 asking it to explain why the said balance sheet be not kept in view for a further period of six months from the receipt of this notice. On April 3, 1969 the appellant was served with a notice under section 148 of the Act calling upon him to showcause why the company should not make any profit and losses account of its company as required by section 220 (1) read with section 220 of the Indian companies Act, 1913. The said notice was replied by the Registrar stating that the balance sheets and profit accounts of the petitioner were not maintained in accordance with the provisions contained in sections 220(2), 220(3) and 220(4) of Companies act 1956. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notice on the ground that it was violative of section 220 read with Section 220 of Companies (Second Amendment) Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that if no balance sheet is laid before a general body, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 221 and though wilful omission to call a general meeting and to lay the balancesheet and profit or loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of this Act, it certainly does not make him liable udder aforesaid provisions. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that (1 ) the decision necessarily led to the conclusion that even in a prosecution under section 134 of the 1913 Act the company and its directors could not rely upon their failure to call the general meeting as a defence to the prosecution; (2) the fact that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to file the list is independent of the holding of a general meetings. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The decision necessarily lead to the inference that even if in a criminal case under section134 of the Old Companies Act the accused would be liable for punishment for that default.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1952. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that the provisions of section 5 (1) were discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution in so far as it purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case, "whether the duration of such a case is likely to be long or not ". The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The object of the Act was that the preamble was to be read as a whole and section 5 of the , did not by its own force make the special procedure provided in the Act applicable to the trial of certain offences. [291 C] (ii) The Special Court had no jurisdiction to try these "cases" of the respondents. The provisions of the section were therefore discriminatory and violated article 14. [292 E F] (iii)The object being, as I have said, different ele ments, it follows that the object by itself cannot be the basis of the classification of offences or the cases, for in the absence of any special circumstances which may dis tinguish one offence or one class of cases from another offence, or class of offences and speedier trial is desirable in the disposal of all offences or classes of cases. [293 G] (iv)The Special Court was not justified in holding that section 5 was discriminatory in so as it authorised the State government to direct "cases". The Act did not make any special provision for the speediers trial of those offences and therefore it was necessary to ascertain whether it was actually based on such a classification.
