The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the post held by him was akin to that of honorary Professor or Associate Professor in a teaching hospital attached to the Ma�ulana Azad medical College and treating as an Assistant Professor of radiotherapy (ex officio). In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant has not acquired the status of an Associate professor of Radiological with effect from October 9, 1964, particularly when the Central Government have been utilizing his services as such for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students of the Maurulana Azad University. [814G] 2.2 The designation of the Appellant as a radiologist cum Assistant Professor in Ma�shi Azad Medical college is akin to the designation of Associate Professor or Radiology (exofficio) by the University of Delhi. The status of Associate Professors of Radiography (ex<+ officio) which the appellant enjoys in the Irwin Hospital is akin, to that as honorary Professor/Assistant professor in the Willing don Hospital or the Safdarjung hospital and the mere designation of a person as such does not give him a right to hold the post. That being so, it was urged that the appellant who was a Radiographer cum Associate professor in Maur Azad Medical University cannot be appointed by direct recruitment as Professor of Diotherapy under r. (2) of the Central Civil Health Service Rules, 1963. [915A B] 2:3 The designation and status of the appellants as a Doctor/Assistant Professors in the Medical Colleges and teaching institutions shall be governed by the Central health Service ( Amendment) Rules, 1966. [1016C D] 2 :4 The appellant is not eligible for appointment to the posts of Associate professor or Radiologist under rs. (1) and (2A) and paragraph 3 of Annexure I to the Second Schedule determine the question of his eligibility for such promotion or appointment. [717E F] 2(a) and para 3 of the Annexure I are, therefore, eligible to be considered for appointment as Associate Professor/Associate Professor in Radiotheraprapy under rule (2). The appellant who is a Radiologists cum Associate Professors in Maul Azad Medical Colleges cannot be heard to say that he has not acquire the status or experience of an Assistant professor of radiology with effectfrom October 9. 1964, especially when the State Government have already been utilizes his services for teaching and the post Graduate and undergraduate students of Maulana Ansari Medical College for the M.D., M.S., D.M.R.T. and M.B.B.,S. courses of studies for the last 17 years. [936G H] 2 (b) The designation, of the petitioner as a Diologist cum Professor of Pathology (Ex officio), by the State of Delhi does not make him eligible for promotion or appoint to the said post of Associate Dean in Ma ul Azad Medical Institution. By parity of reasoning, it is urged that he had acquired the qualification of an Additional Professor of Surotherapy cum Associate Doctor of Radiology with retrospective effect from November 9, 1963, particularly since the Central Govern ment have been utilising his services in the medical colleges and teaching institution for the purpose of teaching the posts graduate and Undergraduate students.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, have come up in this appeal by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal, Orissa. The first and the main point argued was that the Tribunal had committed an error of law in fixing minimum wages in the Company on the basis of the average minimum wage prevailing in other industries in that region which could be compared with the Company 's case. Held, that the principle laid down by this Court in French Motor Car Co., Ltd. vs The Industrial Tribunal was not rigid and it is not necessary that the minimum wage should be fixed at the average level of 'wages in the other comparable industries in the region. In the instant case, however, there was nothing to show that the Company was providing any such amenities which were different from the amenities provided by those concerns in the regions which are being.compared with the company for the purpose of fixation of minimum wage Consequently, it would be more appropriate to compare the total wage packet of the Company with the wage packet received by the workmen of other industries In the case of even the lowest paid clerical staff, to whom dearness allowance is separately payable, the bonus is only calculated on the assumption that their wage is a consolidated wage consisting of the two 678 elements of basic wage and dearness allowance lumped together. The principle which is being applied is the simple one of calculating the bonus payable at the rate of three months ' basic wages in each case and in no case is the dearness allowance taken into account.

The assessee was a partner in a partnership firm. On June 3, 1966 the 1st respondent issued to the assessee a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961 calling upon him to furnish within thirty days from the date of service of the notice a return of his income or the income of such other person during the previous year, in the prescribed form and verified in the manner and setting forth such particulars as may be prescribed. The assessee filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the said notice on the ground that it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Commissioner was satisfied that the assessee had failed to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for that year, income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for the assessment year 19 19. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board of Revenue did not set out any reason for coming to the conclusion that the Income tax Officer had complied with the requirement of section 148 and section 151 (2) and that the notice issued under section 147 was invalid inasmuch as it did comply with all the requirements. HELD : The report submitted by the Income Tax Officer to the Commissioner, it is clear that he could not have had reasons to believe that by reason of the omission or failure on the part of these assessee to disclose truly and truly every material facts essential for his Assessment for that assessment year, the income chargeable chargeable to income tax has escape assessment for any assessment year. [446C D] The report of the Incometax Officer to be vague and indefinite does not mention any reason why he was satisfied with this information in his possession, had reasons or belief that by reasons of the assessee 's omission to disclose full and truly material facts relevant for his assessments for that years income chargeable has escapedassessment for that Year. [427B] The word "yes" is used in section 147(2). It does not mean that it should be construed as a mere possibility or an inference of fact. It means only that the intention of the legislature is to give effect to the intention and object of the legislation. In other words, it must be presumed that the legislature intended to give a meaning to the language used in the statute. [544C D; 548A] The Commissioner has no jurisdiction to issue a notice unders. 148. He did not himself record that he was satisfaction that this is a fit case for the issue of a notice u/s 148.

The appellant was a firm carrying on business in the name and style of Sait Nagjee Purushotham and Co., Bankers, Piece goods and Yarn Merts. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the appellant for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. In appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner the appellant contended that as a result of the splitting up there was a discontinuance of the original business at the date of the partition and on such discontinuance the family became entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the Income tax Act, 1922. Held, that the income, profits and gains of the period between April 13, 1939 and March 28, 1939, were not liable to be taxed in respect of the income profits and gain of the year 1948 50. The business was taxed under the 1918 Act while the emphasis in sub section (4) is on succession to a person who, on April J., 1939, was carrying on any business on which tax was at any time charged under the Act of 1918. The mere fact that he was not taken on in the original 'business also shows that the original partnership business in respect Of which alone the benefit of section 25 (3) could be claimed continued uninterrupted. In the present case there is no succession to the business carried on by the appellant. The only question for consideration was whether the income and profits of the previous year should be deemed to have been the income or profits of that period. Held further, that in terms of business in a business sense, and it is the business which was taxed before the benefit could be obtained. The fact that the appellant was not taking on the original day also shows the existence of a family partition and some vilasams were allotted to the father and the rest to the son, and he was the assessee 's income.

The appellant, a Hindu widow, filed a suit for partition of the coparcenary property in which she was his wife. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit properties belonged to the joint family and that there was no prior partition between her husband and his two sons. On further appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the plaintiff 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband's interest upon his death. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the widow 's right to claim partition or not, was not affected by Explanation 1 to section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, (30 of 1956) as the plaintiff had failed to prove that she was entitled to a share in the interest which her husband had at the time of his death in the coparcenary properties. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : The legal position is well settled that where a partition has taken place between the parties and the property has been divided among them, the heirs will get their or her share in it. [795B] In an important aspect, the case before us is stronger in the matter of working out the fiction because in Teja Singh 's case, a missing step had to be supplied which was not provided for by section 18A(9) if b), namely, the issuance of a notice under section 22 and the failure to comply with that notice. In order to ascertain the share, of the deceased in the property of a deceased coparcener it is necessary in the very nature of things, and as the very first step, to ascertain whether the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in his property that would have been allotted to him if a partition had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled or not.

The appellants were employees of the respondent Corporation. They were governed by the Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960. The Corporation had framed regulations called "the Regulations" for the purpose of regulating the conditions of service of employees of Class I and Class II services in respect of which they were appointed directly to any post belonging to Class I or Class II or Class III categories after 1st September 1956. The Regulations provided that the age of retirement of employees belonging to class I or class II or class III or Class IV shall be 60 years of age but the competent authority may, if it is of the opinion that it is in the interest of the Corporation to do so, direct such employee to retire on completion of 50 years of service or at any time thereafter, if his efficiency is found to have been im paired. The appellants were appointed as Class I employees on 1st August 1956 and they were promoted to Class III posts after 1 st September 1956 by virtue of the settlement and the amendment of the Regulations. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of Regulation 19(2) of the Staff Regulations, which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that clause (b) of section 49(2), was not applicable to the transferred employees who became the employees of Corporation under sub section (1) of Section 11 of the Act but only referred to the employees and agents of the Corpo ration who were employed after 1.9.1956, and who joined service after 1th September 1956 had to retire at 60 years. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: The High Court erred in striking down regulation 19(1) as amended in the year 1977, and in directing the Corporation not to continue the 1st Respondent in its service till he completed the age Of 60 years on his being promoted to a Class I post or ClassII post. [223F] In the instant case, the High ' Court erred by striking down Regulation 19 (2) as it amended in 1965, and directed the Corporation that the employees belonging of Class III and Class IV irrespective of the fact whether they were transferred employees or employees appointed after 1rd September 1956, shall retire on attaining the age o f 60 years or at no time thereafter on giving him three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof. [224F] The High 'Court erred in struck down regulation19(2). [223A B] In view of the clear language of sub section 2 of Section 49(1), it is not possible to accept the contention that clause 4(b) was applicable to transferred employees whose services were directly transferred to Class II posts or Class I posts. The High court erred in holding that the provisions of sub clauses (a) and (b), namely, those appointed subsequent to 1st October 1956, were not entitled to continue in service beyond the age limit of 58 years on their being promoted as Class III employees.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India, the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court. The Chief Justice sent a letter on 20 February 1975 to the Prime Minister, Chief Justice, Haryana High and the Chief Jus tice of Punjab High Court, stating that he had been instructed by the Chief Judge of the High Court to send a notice to the Chief Secretary, Haryana and Haryana high Court for consideration of his apology. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the constitutional validity of the said letter. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the allegations made in the letter were not scandalising the Hon 'ble Judge or the Court in any manner to weaken people ' faith in the administration of justice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the contents of the letter which he and others addressed to the Governor of Punjab, the Prime Ministers did not constitute contempt; (2) the allegations in the letters were vague and indefinite; (3) the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ peti tion. HELD: (i) The letter in question was addressed by the deponent to the Secretary of State for being handed over to him for his personal attention. [246E] (ii) The contents of this letter constituted contempt of court and not a duty in discharge of office of a Judge nor is it a duty In discharge of his duties, a Judge must go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. However, if the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the court would take any action against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech.

The petitioner was a registered dealer under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the petitioner had evaded payment of taxation on income and that the provisions of section 5(1) and (2) of the Act were not attracted to him. He also found that the assessee had failed to pay tax on income. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but reduced the penalty imposed under section 5 (1) of 1922 Act from Rs. 1,000 to Rs. 2,000. The petitioner then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of sub section (4) of section 6 and also the provisions contained in section 7 of the Indian Incometax Act. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the procedure prescribed by the Indian income tax Act was a good substitute for that prescribed by Indian Income Tax Act, and that in any case the procedure laid down by the Act was not a good substituting for that provided by the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the provisions Of section 5 of the , were void because they infringed article 14 of the Constitution; (ii) the procedure to be followed by the Commission is contained in sections 7 and 8 which provide that subject to the provisions thereof, the Commission shall have power to regulate its own procedure and that as such the powers of the Commission under sub section(4) and section 5 were not a part of the present case; (iii) the Act and the impugned Act violated article 14 inasmuch as in any event the procedure for investigation into escaped income or evaded income was limited to a maximum period of eight years, while under the provisions o sub section 4 it is not limited to any period and this certainly operates to the detriment of those dealt with under sub s.(4) Of section 6 of the impugned act; (iv) the impugned sections were void as they infringed articles 19(1)(f), 21 and 22 of the constitution. HELD: (i ) The provisions of sub s. (4), of section 4 and the procedure in the case of persons coming within the ambit of sub cl.(3) of s. 5 are not a piece of discriminatory legislation offends against the provisions in article 20(3)(b). [454 E] (ii ) The entire scheme of the two Acts is to provide for the investigation into the escaped income and evaded income tax by the assessees. It is true that under the Income Tax Laws Act, the same officer who first arrives at a tentative conclusion hears and decides the case, his decision is not final but is subject to appeal, while in the cases of persons falling within the purview of sub clause (4). But the overall picture is that though under the , Indian income Tax Act the same Officer who first arrived at a subjective conclusion heras and decides it, his order is not a final but a quasi judicial one. [454 D] (iii ) The procedure prescribed in section 34 investigation into escape income or evade income is limited to the maximum period and these certainly operate to the prejudice of those dealing with under subsection (4)(a) of Section 5 of Act. [453 E F] (iv ) The overall picture was that though, under the . Indian Incometax Act the matter is referred to the Commission it is the prima facie belief of the Government that enables the reference to be made to the Central Government and the Commission has after investigation to form an opinion; while in case of person coming within section 5 the Commission itself finds and gathers reason to believe that these persons have evaded income Tax and on its report the Government is bound to refer their cases to the same Commission who has.

The appellant, a "commercial establishment" carried on in the premises in question. The Federation was registered under the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. It was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling goods. In the course of its activities, the Federation had been carrying on various kinds of trade and commerce. The Association was formed for the purpose of carrying on certain types of trade or business in connection with, or incidental to, the objects of the Federation. The appellant was a "Commercial Establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act which, in consequence had no application. "The Federation failed to comply with the direction and contended that it was not an "establishment" as defined in section 2 (9) of that Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the activities carried on by the Federation were a business or trade. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The definition of "commercial Establishment" in section2(j) of is far wider than that of " commercial establishment". [352A B] 2.1 It is immaterial whether its activities bring its premises within the ambit of a "shop" or a " commercial Establishment" because by the Memorandum of Association, Articles of Association and other material, which was more or less the same as in the present case, it was held that these activities of the appellant were also in the nature of material services within the wider definition of 'commercial establishment". The fact of the matter is that the Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and issues the same to member free of this Court in R. K. Of course, that profit is ploughed back for the purposes of the Union as set out in its Memorandum of association, and is not distributed among its members. [352C D] 2:2 The mere word "trade" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. It will bear repetition that the definition of the word "business" in s.2(h) of Act is far narrower than that in section. 2(j). [352B C] 3:3 In the instant case, before the High Court, it had not argued that the activity of the Association was not a "trade", business or profession. The fact that the respondent is a Federation of Federations and not an association of any individual traders, industrialists or businessmen cannot, by any stretch of reasoning, be called a "business". [353C D; 353A] 4:4 In the very definition of a 'commercial Establishment", it indicates that the function of a registered society, charitable or other trust will not take it out of the definition if the activity carried on is a business. It would bear repetition to say that the mere word 'trade ' does not automatically mean something By which a profits is made, and it will bear added that the concept of mere word is used in the Act. [353F] 5:5 The fact whether the activities of a Federation are also in nature of materials services within its wider definition indicates that these activity of a society, Charitable or other Trust will not come within the definition unless the activity carries on business or commerce. It does not mean something which by itself amounts to a busi (1)[1971] 1 S.C.R. Mittal 's case, ; , referred to.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of certain lands. The Income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. He observed that "in fact this income arose from a statutory obligation of the Government to pay it, and though the Government recouped this from the person with whom the land was settled, land in the genealogical tree of Malikana appears in the second degree, its immediate and effective source is the Government 's statutory obligation to pay the same, and that is so, notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the income, a substantial part whereof is derived from lands used for agricultural purposes. " The Appellate Tribunal held that the right which was conferred by the letter dated July 7, 1837, no right in the land revenue was granted to the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the income of a trust appropriated by the Government for extinguishing proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of the Income was not land or rent collections from land, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the respondent was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. HELD: (i) The right conferred on a person by an instrument of trust is a right to receive and appropriate to himself the income or revenue of land, but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. [739 E] (ii) The source of income is clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and, therefore it is not agricultural income as defined in the Act; and (iii) the receipt was merely a measure, and indicated the source of this right in lieu of which the allowance was given. [758 D] (iii)(a) The income of an assessee is not taxable under the Indian Income tax Act. It is true that the income can be held to be derived from land within the ambit of the definition in section 2(1)(a). But in this case no material has been produced to show that the allowance varied from year to year, the source and character of the receipt are, therefore, altered when a part of the net income of trust was appropriated by him as his remuneration. [759 E F] (b) The amount of pension is not received by the assessee as rent or revenue. It follows from the decisions of the Privy Council and the judgments of this Court cited above that if it is held in this particular case that the source is clearly arrangement arrived into in 1838, then the income cannot be held income derived from the land within its meaning of the term in section 4 (3)(ix) of Income tax.

The petitioners in the writ petitions claim to have been appointed as Supervisors Gra de 'A ' in various ordnance factories between 1962 to 1966 a nd had filed these writ petitions with the prayer that they be granted promotion to higher posts. The respondents in the said writ petitions claimed that they were entitled to be treated as Chargeman II on completion of 2 years ' service as Supervisor 'A and that their promotion thereafter could be effected only in accordance with the normal rules. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the petitioners of this appeal had not been promoted as Chargemen II on expiry of 2 yea rs of continuous service on the basis of the circular dated 6th November, 1962 and circular dated 20 th January, 1966. In the appeals to this Court it was contended for the respondents that since Rule 8 of the Rules contemplated a post by promotion were to be made on the ground of completion of two years ' servi ce as Supervisor A ' by its order dated 16th April, 1979, there was no scope for automatic promotion merely because some Supervisors having been en promoted as chargeman II and some others had even been promoted to higher post. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellants of this case have in purs u ance of the order of this Court dated 2nd February, 1981 been given a back date promotion to the post of Chargeman Grade II on completing two years of service as Supervisors Grade A. 441 of 1981 are disposed of by issuing a direction to the respondents to give them in the aforesaid Civ il Appeal the same benefits as were granted by the Madhya Pradesh High Court to such of the petitioners before that Court wou ld be granted to the 109 petitioners before this Court w ho were Supervisors 'A, and were granted promotion as Chargem an II by its judgment dated 4th April 1983. [441C D] 1.2 The appellants in Civil Appeal No. 441/81 may also be granted the same relief which was granted to them by the High Court. As regards back wages the Madhya Prade sh High Court held that the appellants of the appeal have in due course been en en promoted to the higher post with effect fr om the date their junior was promoted. [442D] 1:3 The appellants have in this case not been able to show any rule or circular which would govern the matter. They have also not been given promotion as chargemen II.1 In view of the fact that they have not been granted promotion, they cannot claim to be deemed Chargeman I on completion o f two years service as Charge man II.2 It is now settled law that there has to be no p ay for no work i.e. a person will not be entitled to any p ays and allowance during the period for which he did not perfo rm the duties of a higher post although after due considerati on he was given a proper place in the gradation list havi ng deemed to be promoted to that higher post though after due consideration o he was give a proper date in theradation list hav ing deemed to have be en promoted. The appellants cannot claim any right to be considered for promotion merely on completion or completion of three years ' services as Charge Man II by their order dated 6 11 1966. [444E F] 1 :3.1 It is settled service rule that there can be no work in a person would not be entitle to any benefit during the periods for which they did not complete the duties. The question whether an employee will be entitled only on completionof two years or not, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case.

The Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation, the appellant in these appeals, was granted permits for operating in any inter State route. The State Transport Undertaking applied for stage carriage permit from a State Transport undertaking for operating on the route. On the basis of the said application, the State Transport Authority granted permits to the private operators. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the permits and also the validity thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the proviso to section 63(7) did not offend article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the State transport Appellate Tribunal and the High court were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Singh 's case and that the fourth sub clause of the proviso was unconstitutional and violative of article 14. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1 H) does not mean mere passing of an approved scheme or a notification by the State Government to the effect that it would be effective from the date on which the scheme is sanctioned. [1015C] 2. The proviso to sec. 63(1) does no say for example, like section 68 F(1), that the permit shall be granted to the State Undertaking. It only provides that in the case of inter State routes, the Undertaking will have preference in the matter of stage carriage permits. [ 1015C D] 3. The general scheme of the Act in the context of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the cases of a notified route or notified area, where under section 68F(1)(a) the permit has to be necessarily granted to such State Transport Undertakings in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. [1005D] 4. The words 'preferably grant ' occurring therein cannot mean mere making of an application for stage Carriage permit from one State to another. It is not necessary that the applicant should have a certificate of approval from the Central Government because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to Section 63(2). [1016E] 5. The expression 'preferential grant ' appearing in section 68D(1H) does mean only an application made for stage transport permit from another State Transport Corporation and not a mere application for a stage carriage Permit. It does not say, for example that like section68 F(I)(a), the permit had to be invariably granted to a State transport Undertaking. [102E] 6. The sub clause (iv) of the provisos to section63(7), is unconstitutional and it cannot be said that the application made by the applicant for stage stage carriage stage carriage was not for tourist vehicles or travel agents. [103F G] 7. The second proviso to s. 63 (7) is unconstitutional, and it is struck down as violative of Article 14 of Constitution. [104G H] 8. The third proviso to sub section (7), does not state that the permits shall be given preference overall other applications. It merely provides for preference to be given under section 47 (1H).

The respondent purchased a business in the name of M/s. Ram Reddy, who was carrying on the business of selling goods and sales tax was payable by the appellant. The Sales Tax Officer held that the respondent had no authority to impose sales tax on the sale of goods sold by him. He also imposed penalty under section 7(1) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 (Madras Act IX of 1939). In appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the respondent contended that the State Government had power under section 19(1)(c) of Madras Act IX Of 1939 to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the business was constituted as the dealer liable to pay the tax in respect of his turnover and under the scheme of the charging provision of the Act the purchaser of the goods sold must have nothing to do with the sales effected by him, that the sale was not for the purpose of earning income from the sale. Held, that under section 3(1), the State Legislature has power to frame rules to carry out the purposes of the enactment and it is beyond the rule making power of the State government either under section 18 or 19(2)(c). The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2) (c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule 21 A is beyond its rule making powers of the state Government either under sections 19(I) and (2), of the, Act. Ganapathy Iyer on behalf of the respondent that there was no undertaking on the part of the appellant to discharge the liabilities in regard to arrears of sales tax due by the transferor, it does not follow 66 7 that there is a liability created inter se between the State Govt on the one hand and the transferee on the other hand.

The appellant was a public servant. He was dismissed from service on the ground that it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution. The State of Gujarat appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) The liability to pay arrears of salary earned by a public Servant for the period that he was actually in office is the liability of the State of Bombay and not of the Government servant for the time during which he has served. [922 D] (ii) The decree of the High Court decreeing payment of arrears of pay is truly a liability in proceedings relating to a contract within section 60(2)(a). It is true that some elements of relationship between a public officer and Government are based on contracts within the meaning of section 60 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. But so far as the State is concerned, some elements are of relationship inter se between a private servant and Government servants within the ambit of section 61. [ 922 E] (iii) The words ,actionable wrong other than breach of contract ' in this context are wide words and include something more than torts, but even so where a suit is brought by a Government servant against arrears of wages, the decree more properly falls under section 60. [961 D] In the instant case, the plaintiff was not concerned with the second contention but it was a dispute between the State and the State Government of Gujarat. The liability for payment of salary was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability which in fact arose wholly within the territory of the state of Maharashtra or the State.

The appellants were owners of certain land. The respondents ' predecessor in interest, made an inquiry and came to know that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the southern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. The plaintiffs alleged that the respondents had encroached on their coal mine on the northern side and removing coal from them and had thereby rendered the entire land of the encroachment impossible. The trial court held that the defendant had encroached over the appellants ' leasehold land, that the suit was not barred by limitation and that they would be entitled to the reliefs prayed for. On appeal, the High Court held that article 48 applied to the suit and that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondent had knowledge of the sinking of the quarries and pits in the encroached land. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the finding of fact arrived at by the courts below was erroneous as the initial burden was on the respondents to prove the possession of the converted property within three years thereof. Held, that article48 of the Limitation Act applied to a suit and the appellant could not claim any benefit under article 48 of the Indian Limitation Act. The onus of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondents beyond the prescribed time was on them. The burden of proving that they had knowledge about the sinking or pits in their encroached land was on him. In other words, he has to prove by showing that he obtained the knowledge of his possession within three year of the date of the filing of the suit.

The appellant was a crosscutter. The Secretary and others were charged with misconduct under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the ground that it was not a bona fide exercise of the power conferred by r. 19(a). Held, that the Industrial Court had the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(A) and if it is satisfied that the action taken under such a rule was a colourable exercise of power and was not bona fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. The Industrial Court in its opinion had the power to inquire from the causes which might have lead to termination and if the terminaton of service is a colourable exercising of the powers conferred, it would be an colourable exercise Of the power under that rule. In the present case the tribunal held that the exercise of powers was colourable and it could not be said that view was incorrect. The Tribunal had the jurisdiction to inquire whether there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action was taken under r 18(b) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was misconduct and, therefore, the action took under r, 18(c) was bona fide and was therefore not colourable exercise. The employer could defend the action under r., 18(d). Held further, that in a case of this kind the requirement of bona fides is essential and if an employee wants to take action for misconduct and then suddenly dropped the departmental proceedings which were intended to be held and decided to discharge the employee under r . 18(e) it is now well settled that even in a cases where the employer wanted to take disciplinary action against an employee instead of following the course of holding an inquiry for misconduct actually charged might be done away with. The industrial court cannot inquire into causes that may have led a result to termination.

The appellants were the tenants of a building in Ahmedabad. The respondent landlord filed a suit for declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated December 1, 1960, to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre and for an injunction restraining the defendants from violating the said rights of Filmistan under the agreement. The Trial Court held that the consent decree had not decided that the transaction between the parties of the year 1954 was in the nature of a lease; that the suit No. 149 of 1960 was for declaration of the rights of the Filmistans to exhibit Motion pictures in theatre under the terms of the said agreement dated November 27, 1954 and for injunction restraining defendants from interfering with their possession. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the question whether the legal relationship arising out of the agreement between December 1. 1960 was in existence or not was decided by the consent order of December 1., 1960; that in the plaint in the earlier suit it was not even averred that the rights granted were in the character of leasehold rights; that it related to a matter to be decided by a Court and on which the opinion of witnesses was irrelevant. The appellants contended that the agreement was not a lease ? HELD : (i) The question whether in fact the subordinate Court has decided the question of res judicata is one which is not vested in it by law. [419 C] (ii)The order passed by the High Court is set aside and the Trial Court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [420 B] (iii)The question whether a legal relationship arose out of an agreement dated October 27, 1955 was already concluded by the Consent decree in suit No 149 of 1961. The only thing that can be said is that so far as the agreement of November 27. 1954 is con cerned, it must be held, in view of the consent judgment of December l., 1960, that that document created a lease. [ 420 E] (iv)The High Court has recorded a finding that the document dated November 28, 1954 created a tenancy and that the said consent decree operated as res judicata. The order passed in suit no 149 of 1958 had not been decided that it did not decide that question. It was for the Trial court to decide whether the transaction was in fact barred by res judicata or estoppel under the provisions of section 92 of the Evidence Act. [416 G H] (v)The Court has not recorded a findings on the question as to whether the document executed was a lease or of other character had to be determined at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent , 'could not operate as resjudicata, for it was only a finding of fact. [414 G] (vi)The agreement dated March 27,1954 created a leasehold interest in the cinema theatre under which the appellants were tenants. The document created lease was not one of the conditions precedent to the applicability of section 28 of the Bombay Rent Control Act. It did not create any tenancy or right in the building.

The respondent was appointed as a Pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was working as a pilot Officer. In the year 1972 he was declared unfit by a Medical Board and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State of Uttar Pradesh also adopted the same scheme. The term of the respondent had come to an end on 30th August, 1985 as stated above and no further order of extention had been passed by the Governor. In this connection it was contended that the interim order granted in favour of the respond ent was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30th of August,1985 were liable to be ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to con tinue till he completed the age of 58 years. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ petition was liable tobe dismissed. In appeal by special leave it was submitted on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had while setting aside the order of termination by its order dated 24th March, 1988 directed that the respondent was entitled to salary upto the period he was entitled for remain in service and further observed that it was open for the opposite parties to consider the claim of the petitioner for continu ation in service or of fresh appointment and no observations in this regard were made by the Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent had not urged before the High court that the order dated 9th July, 1986 passed in his case was not an order of extension of service. If the respond ed was really aggrieved by the judgment dated 24.3.1988 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that was not right in making an order on Review on 26.7.1988 relying upon the interim orders dated 10th July 1986 passed by this Court during the pendency of the Writ Appeal. [243E F] 2. The interim order did not and could not amount to a direction that the respondents were entitled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the merits of the case and the extent of his right. [244F] 3. The order dated 10.7,.86 passed by High Court on review and restore the Judgment dated 24/3. 1988 passed in the Writ Petitions. The Interim order did neither and could have been amount to an direction that he was not entitled to remain in serv beyond 30th September, 1985 unless there was a further extension. [245G] 4. The writ petition was dismissed by this court on the ground of delay. [246F] 5. In view of the fact that no order of 'extension had been sanctioned by the Government beyond 30.8.1985, the respondent could not have filed an appeal against the judgment of the High Curt. The stay order did nothing but only a direction to the effect that the Respondent was entitled only to remain on service till he attained the age Of 58 years and further directed that he be treated in service even though there was no order from extension of services.

The appellant was acquitted by the Additional Sessions judge, Chittoor of an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code. The High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted him under section 304 Part I read with section 34 Indian Penal code. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the accused had no motive to kill his wife and that his version was more probable than the version of the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of the eye witnesses is not sufficient to sustain the conviction of an accused person. [368B] 2. The medical evidence does not support the prosecution case as it has been corroborated by the evidence of P.W. 3 and that the doctor who examined the deceased had found the injuries on her body. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. [369C] 3. The prosecution tried to make P. W. 1 prepared by P. Ws. 9, 10 and 11 who had gathered there also gave a beating to the accused. It was obvious that the motive would assume considerable importance if the case was one based on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution tried in to make him guilty of murder. [370D] 4. The doctor who treated the deceased as an injured witness has not been examined by the prosecution and the defence has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [372F] 5. The trial court had rightly convicted the appellant under section302 Indian Penal Penal Code, but the High Court was well justified in commenting that the discrepancies noticed by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character and that they have been unduly magnified by the learned Sessions Judge. [371C] 6. In the instant case, the evidence on record does not show that the prosecution had tried to create any doubt about the veracity of the testimony of P 1 to 3 or the evidence given by the defence witnesses on the basis of which the Trial Court rejected the evidence. The accused was acquitted under section 324 Indian Penal Procedure. [373F] 7. In view of the above, it is not possible to accept the contention that an injury of the nature received could have been caused in the manner suggested by the accused and that where the trial court allows itself to be beset with fanciful doubts, rejects creditworthy evidence for slender reasons and takes a view of his evidence which is but barely possible.

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court and was holding office as such. He was appointed as Chief Justice of India in the year 1962. The Chief Justice, after considering the recommendations of the Committee of Judges, recommended that the Chief Justice be appointed to the post of Chief Justice or Chief Justice. In his report dated May 5, 1963, the Chief Judge stated that he had no power to appoint a Judge or Chief Judge of a High Court unless he was satisfied that there were sufficient grounds for doing so. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the Chief Justices as Judges of the High Courts. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the sanction under section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 is not necessary to prosecute a Judge under the provisions of the said Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that for the purpose of deciding the question of applicability of the Act to the appellant as a Judge, the office with reference to which the offence under the Act is alleged to have been committed, it is necessary to consider the feasibility of grant of sanction under Section 6(i)(c). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power to punish a High court Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in article 2 18 read with article 124(4) and (5) of that Constitution for removal of the Judge. [216C D] 2.1 The incumbent of the office of Chief Judge exercises only moral authority over his colleagues in the Supreme court and the High court Judges which has no legal sanction behind it making it justiciable. It appears that the framers of the Constitution while dealing with such constitutional functionaries, contemplated merely their removal from office in the manner provided in Article 124(5) as the only punishment; and a special law enacted by the Parliament under Article 124 (5), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior Judge instead of the general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. The incumbent, of the Office of Chief Justices exercises only administrative power over his subordinates in the discharge of their duties. [217D E] 2:2 It is for this reason that the Parliament did not enact any other law even then for the investigation into allegations of corruption against a subordinate Judge and for his trial and punishment for that offence and rest content merely with enacting the , to provide for the procedure for remov al of a Judge. The obligation of the Court to consider such feasibility is clearly visualized when the allegation is connected With his office, and for that matter even to the High Judges, since the ChiefJustice of India is not a vertical superior of any of them, there being no such vertical hierarchy and the Chief Judges of India having no legal authority behind it make it justiciable.[217D F] 2(a) The incumbent has to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction under Article124(4). [218G H] 3:3. The requirement of the provision is that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under Section 5 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952 except in the mode envisaged in Article 125(5), clauses (4) & (5). This is not the position in the case of removal of a judge. [218F G] 4:4. The provision is inappliable to a Judge who is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference thereto which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste and not a member. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground that Abhoy Pada was a "untractive caste" and not as a member or a member belonging to a Scheduled Caste. The Election Tribunal held that Abhyudaya Pada belonged to a smaller caste group within the Sunri caste, distinguished itself by their surname, whatever might be his other characteristics". The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that Abdoy P.ada was not a "Untractive" and that it was not open to him at the trial to contend as he appeared to have done. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The word 'Saha ' in item 40 must, without more, also refer to a caste group of Sahas. [391 E] (2) The Tribunal came to its conclusion that Abnoy Putta was a Sunri by caste and did not belong to the Scheduled Caste specified in item 39. [392 G] (3) The appellant was not proved to belong to 'the Scheduled Caste ' specified in Item 40, though he was a 'untramactive caste. The evidence clearly established that the appellant belonged to the Saha group of a Sahas and did neither belong to that caste nor were he within that caste who formed the smaller caste Group of Saha. [393 C] (4) The respondent called witnesses to establish that the Sahas formed a sub caste strictly so called within the ' Sunri Caste '. The appellant, therefore, did not belonged to 'Untra operative caste ' and set aside the judgment of the High Court and restore that of the Election Tribunal dismissing the election Petition. [394 D] (5) The evidence before it did not establish that Abhya Pada had been admitted by the respondent and, therefore did not belongs to the community specified in items 40 and 43.

The appellant was a tenant of the premises in question. The appellant had been paying rent to the respondent for the use and occupation of the flat. The police party, who were down below ready for the raid, held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 29,500 as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The Police party, however, recovered the bunch of keys and the documents that were handed over to him by the appellant. The complainant was further charged under section 19(2) of the Act for receiving the said sum as a term of art and was also charged under sections 19(1)(a), (b) and (c) of Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The prosecution case is that the appellant wanted to go to the United Kingdom for treatment of his failing eye sight and he got into touch with the complainant Mulchand Kodumal Bhatia, who was also to act as caretaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view that he entered into negotiations with the complain ant. The evidence on record shows that the police party had recovered the entire bunch of key and the document that were given to him through the appellant, namely, the letter handing vacant possession (Exhibit D). The police also recovered the documents which were handed back to the complainant. The Magistrate convicted the appellant under section 20(2)(a) of Act and sentenced him to one day 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs 2,000 for the furniture, and that the complainant agreed to pay these sums. On appeal by the appel lant the High Court acquitted the appellant but reduced the sentence to one month 's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appell ant that the offence arose only on receipt of any sum or any consideration as a condi tion from a tenant and that in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary, he entered in negotiations with him. HELD: (1) The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary in the present case, in the light of section 108, sub clause (i), of the Trans fer of Property Act. [446 B] (2) The relinquishment of a tenancy is equivalent to surrender by the lessee or tenant of his rights as such. The other parts of the order of the learned Presidency Magistrate, as regards the disposal of Rs 1,000 paid by the complainant to the appellant will, however stand.

The appellant, who maintained a wage scale of Rs. 150/ and Rs. 100/ in the category of Draftsmen and Rs 150/ in that category of Draughtsman and Rs 200/ in other categories, was entitled to get a flat increase of Rs 150/- in the class of Draftsman and also to pay dearness allowance and there was no mention of giving any ad hoc increase in the basic pay of individual workmen. The appellant maintained that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Industrial Tribunal, however, held that the revised wage scales had necessarily to commence with figures Rs.150/ and that there was nothing in the body of the award to form the foundation on which the actual figures in the restructured pay scales could be made to rest. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the Union that the expression "flat increase" occurring in section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, means a change in the existing conditions of service and not an alteration in the conditions of services of the employees. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The word "filter increase" is used in the sense that it includes a change of conditions of employment or change of condition of service. [176C] 2. The expression "instead of any work or class of workmen" in section 3(k), means an alteration of conditions and conditions of work, which is not intended to be altered by the employer. It is only when there is a change that the conditions are changed by the employee. In the instant case, the Industrial Tribunal had merely revised the wage scales by increasing the salary on entry into the service and res 184 tructuring the scale of pay and never granted any adhoc increase in salary to all employees. The omission of the words to each employee first after the figure Rs. 200/ and again after the figures were Rs. 151/ and thereafter after the word figure Rs 150 / was added to the pay of every other workman, who belonged to the Union staff, the financial load would increase to Rs. 50/ in addition to the existing wages scales. Immediately after the award was pronounced, while the iron was still hot as it were, the employees apparently realised that the employer might take advantage of the circumstance that it was not clearly mentioned in the award that all the employees were to get additional pay of Rs, 150/ or Rs.100/ respectively and might contend that the Tribunal had only revised the wages by increasing its salary on Entry into the Service and never granting any ad adhoc increase of salary to All employees. [177D E] 3. The words "in stead of anything done in pursuance of this award" occurring therein, mean an alteration or change in conditions of labour or service or change or condition of work which is necessary for the proper implementation of the provisions of the Act. [178C D] 4. In making the award dated December 20, 1978 the Tribunal was betrayed by a curious confusion in accepting the plea of the appellant that a flat increased to the Pay of each individual workman was intended in the original wage and, consequently, it fell into the error of amending the award. The omissions of the word "Filter increases" are clearly intended by the Tribunal as is evident from the reference to "fat increase of pay". [177E F] 5. In view of the clear statement of its intention, the Tribunal thought that an all round flat increase in Rs. 250/ andRs. 100 / was meant to each of the workmen who belonged, to the union staff, and the other categories.

The appellant was employed as a driver in the respondent company. The respondents were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 250 per day. The appellant paid its employees only As. / 10 / 10/ per day and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The employer contended before the authority that the refusal of the appellant to pay to them wages at a rate awarded in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant, to pay the said prescribed wages. Held, that the terms prescribed by an award could not be included. The terms prescribed in an award, in law, constitute a fresh contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that even under the unamended definition of wages, rates of remuneration prescribed by the award could also not be excluded. It was then well settled that where an award made by an Industrial Tribunal cannot be said to amount to a contract of employment, the wage structure prescribed by it must be deemed to be a contract between employers and workmen make it reasonable to think that even though the period of operation of the award and the period for which it remained binding on the parties may elapse in respect of both of which special provisions have been made under sections 23 and 29 respectively the new contract would continue to govern the relations between the employer and the employees. The words " wages" in section 2(vi) of the , must be read as including wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudication, and since an award passed by an industrial tribunal cannot be treated as wages under section 2 (vi), it is not open to the Industrial Court to interfere with that award.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed certain works at a place called Karhali. The trial Magistrate convicted him both under section 465 and section 409 I.P.C. and sentenced him to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by the State to the High Court, the appellant contended that sanction was necessary under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for prosecution under section misappropriation of funds and that there having been an acquittal of the appellant by the trial Magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate Court. Held: (i) The prosecution which has resulted in the conviction of the accused was initiated without sanction under section 196(1). The charge against him was framed without any sanction under s 197(2) of Code of Civil Procedure and if sanction under that section is necessary, as contended for by Mr. According to the respondent, however, the main charge against the appellant was under section 408 I. P.C., and no sanction was required for a prosecution under that Section. (ii) The mere fact that the accused did not pay the amount to Parma, and the acquittance roll records the payment, and there is in acknowledgment thereof a thumb impression as against his name. If what appears on the face of the roll is true and whether it is true or not is not a matter relevant at the stage of sanction then the acts with which the appellant is charged fall within the scope of his duties, and can be justified by him as done by virtue of his office. (iii) The sanction was not necessary under s. 197(l) of Criminal P. C., for prosecution of the person doing it, that he could not, when charged with it, claim justification for it by virtue Of his office, that therefore no sanction under the section was necessary and that the question was concluded by the decisions in Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor (1) and Albert We8 Meads vs The King (2), in both of which the charges were of criminal misappropriation.

The assessee was a resident of Travancore State in the erstwhile State of Cochin. The income tax authorities included the profits of the business and assessed them to income tax under section 12B of the Travancore Income tax Act, Travancore. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business losses incurred in the former State could be set off against the business profits made in British India or Travancore State as the case may be. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the first proviso to section 24(1) of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1941, did not apply to the present case because the word " income" used in the proviso to sub section (2) of section 14 of the Act did not include business losses which were incurred in British country or in an Indian State and that the words " loss of profits or gains arising from him within the meaning of clause (e) of sub section(2) Of section 18 of the Income tax, 1922, were used in relation to business or vocation carried on by a resident outside India. Held, that the mere use of the words loss of profit or gains to be, set off under section 10 must mean business in British Indian States only and not to any other section. The mere fact that the word ' income " is not used does not justify the construction. that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising under the head business in the two territories, i. e., British India and the Indian States.

The respondent company was a public limited company. The Company had been to retire its employees at the age of 55. In September, 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees in Calcutta under which the age for retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. The workmen 's case that the trend in Bombay region had been about fixing the retirement age at 60 years was not challenged before this Court In Imperial Chemical Industries 427 (India) Private Ltd., vs The Workmen, ; , relied on. Held, further, that the Tribunal had failed to notice the fact that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay regions the trend had been at fixing the retire age at 58 subject to certain employees passing the medical examination and reaching the superannuation age of 60. In the present case an attempt appears to have been made on behalf of the respondent Company to show that it was not correct to say that the error in the Bombay region was a mere device to fix the retirement date of retirement at 60. The Tribunal had found that in some of the awards there was a general agree ment that the age should be fixed at 60 and not at 55. On a consideration of all the facts and circumstances disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on this record, it was clear that the decision of the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem was not very commendable. The Court had failed in regard to the fact of the age as stated by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in appeal, was in fact inaccurate.

The appellants were the managing agents of M/s Barium Chemicals Ltd. and M/S Barium Chemical Works Ltd., who were directors of M. P. Industries Ltd. The first respondent was the managing agent of M P. Industrial Corporation Ltd. (the appellant) and the second respondent was its managing agent. The second respondent passed an order under section 237(b) of the Act directing the appellants to appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The appellants challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that it was not competent to pass an order in exercise of its power under section 240(b). Held, that the discretion conferred on the Central Board by section 237 (b) to order an investigation and delegated by it to the Company Law Board is administrative, that it could be validly exercised by the Chairman of the Board by an order made in pursuance of a rule enacted by the Central Legislature under section 642(1) read with section 10E(5), that the exercise of the power does not violate any fundamental right of the appellants and its members. The power conferred on a Central Government by section 238(b), to order investigation and delegate by it, is administrative; that it can be validly delegated by the Board but it has no power to authorise the Chairman to sub delegate this function to himself and consequently, the Company law Board (Procedure) Rules, 1964 made by the State Government on February 6, 1964 and the Chairman 's order of distribution of business dated February 6 1964 delegating the functions of the board under section 239 to the Chairman are ultra vires the and the impugned order is invalid.

The assessee firm applied to the Tribunal under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 for referring the following question to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off as irrecoverable in the books of account was not one incurred in the course of money lending business of the assessee ?" The Tribunal rejected the application but pursuant to an order made by the High court under section 67(2) submitted a statement of the cases on the following questions " Whether on the findings and in law, the Income tax Officer was right In law in disallowing the debt. " HELD : (i) The debt in question was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending trade or business nor a debt representing loss sustained in the other business. [12 E] (ii) The Tribunal has found that the monies sent by the assessee to the Bombay firm were not loans made in the ordinary course of their money lending, but in respect of any other business of assessee. It is true that the amounts sent by them to the Madras firm were neither loans made nor in respect thereof. [13 E F] (iii) The amount sent by it to the Calcutta firm was not loans advanced in the normal course of its moneylending business nor in regard to any other income of the appellant. [14 G H] (iv) The amounts sent to the Delhi firm were never loans made, but only in respect o loans made by that firm in the usual course of the money lending businesses. It was not an "accommodation" account to enable the Bombayfirm to tide over the "financial crisis". [15 E F].
