The petitioners in these petitions are the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Sections 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Act, 1976 (hereinafter referred to as "the Bangalore Act"). Under the provisions Of Section 36 of the Karnataka Act, where the acquisitions, otherwise than by agreement, it will be regulated by the provisions as far they are applicable. The lands in question were acquired for the purpose of construction of a building and a construction thereon. Under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (hereinafter called "the Land Acquisition) Act, the Collector must make his award within two years from the date of publication of the declaration and that if no award is made within that period, the entire proceedings for acqui sation of the land shall lapse. The respondents in these writ petitions are also the owners. In these writ petition, the petitioners have sought to challenge the acquisition of the lands by way of a Writ Petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The Karnataka High Court granted interim stay of dispossession therein and granting interim stay against dispossession therefrom. The Petitioners preferred Special Leave Petitions against the decision of a learned Single Judge in the appeals filed by them before this Court. Dismissing the petitions, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are owners of some lands which had been acquired by them under the Land acquisition Act. Under Section 36A of the Land Acquis tive Act, they were entitled to compensation for the acquired lands. They obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to possession of the said lands in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the order of the High Court dated August 14, 1984. On December 16, 1987, two writ petitions were filed by the respective petitioners in the Karnataka High court challenging the acquisition on the ground that the awards in these cases had not been made within the stipulated time. The said interim stay orders were vacated by a Division Bench of that High Court on November 29, 1988. In the meantime, the respondents appeared in response to the notice and filed their counter affidavit. In those writ petitions, they sought to raise an objection regarding non disclosure of the same. They also sought to quash the acquisition proceedings on the grounds that the award was not made within two months of the date on which the stay orders had been vacated by the High court. The State Government filed a counter affidavit contending that as the awards were not made in time, they could not challenge the validity of the acquisition. It was contended on behalf of the respondents that as there was no reference in the Special Leave petitions to any stay order and the non disclosure thereof would amount to suppression of material facts. That contention was repelled along with certain other contentions in the judgment of the Division Bench which is sought to be impugned before this court. In view of the provisions contained in Section 36 A of the Act, it was beyond dispute that the fact of the stay order was highly material in the determination of these Special Leave Appeals. The High Court allowed the petitions and granted interim relief staying further proceedings in respect of the acquisitions. It is well settled in law that the relief under Article 136 of the constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. [501G H; 502A B] 2.1 In view Of the provisions in Section 11 A of Land Ac quis tions Act, 1984, it would be governed by the principles as far as they are not applicable. [603C D] 3.2 The respondents have sought for quashing the acquisition and granting Interim stay against possession therefrom. They have also sought for a declaration that they were not entitled to any compensation. The Respondents in these Writ Petitions are also owners of lands which have been acquired under the Karnataka Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act 1984.

The appellant bank was a nationalised bank. The workmen were drawing basic pay at the rate of Rs. 250 per month. The Sastry award provided that the workmen would be fitted in the new scales of pay from January 1, 1962 on stage to stage adjustment basis, i.e., workmen who entered service of the bank before 1st January 1959 shall not be reduced in any case. The appellant bank filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the award and also the validity or otherwise of the Sastry award. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Sastry Award provided that "the workmen would work in the old scales of Rs 250 per year as on January 1 1959, and that they would be entitled to increments under sub cl. (a) of cl. 182. Held, that the High court was right in holding that it had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ application. The award provided for a revision of the existing scales of dearness allowance and the revision of pay scale. The revision of scales of Dearness Allowance and the revisions of pay scales were not governed by the Sastry Awards Award. The Desai Award provided for revision of existing scales and the revised pay scale was to be fixed as on February 1, 1959. The scheme of the Desai award was that the scales of allowances in the existing grades would be revised from time to time. The variation in the scales was not a matter of course. It was only with reference to the scales which were earlier fixed by the Desai Award. There was no provision for revision and it was not open to the Sastry Tribunal to revise the scales. The present case was covered by cl. 5. (ii) of the National Industrial Tribunal (Bank Disputes) Award, the adjusted basic pay in the revised scale was not to exceed what point to point adjustment would give an employee on January1, 1959, as modified by placing him at the stage in the Sastry awards scale equal to or next above his basic pay as on 1st February 1959.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain land in Calcutta, applied for a lease of the land on the ground that the Zoo could not be run for a single day without the essential services which were being provided in the four acres of land proposed to be given for the hotel. The respondent State Government granted the lease of Begumbari land to the Taj Group of Hotels for the construction of Five Star Hotel. The appellants challenged the validity of the lease on the grounds that the decision to lease the Begumbar land to them was taken on February 12, 1981 and that the said decision was arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The Division Bench held that the Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of the zoo when they decided to grant four acres out of four acres. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the interests and the requirements of the Zoological Garden were totally ignored and not kept in mind while passing the decision. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Government was very alive to this need for the expan ny of theZoo when it decided to lease a land to respondent No. 2. [263G] 1.2 In view of the State Policy, there would be no question of any resin being sold in the open market. the object of the Government in such a case is not to earn revenue from sale of resin, but to promote the setting up of industries within the State and invite those interested to come up with pro posals for the purpose. The object of State in such an event is not only to earn revenues from sale or distribution of resin but also to promote setting up industries within tapping contract simpliciter there can be no doubt that the State would have to auction or invite tenders for securing the highest price, subject, of course, to any other relevant overriding considerations of public interest. But in a case like this where the State is allo cating resources such as water, power raw materials etc. for the purposes of encouraging setting up otheuuu uries within the state, we do not think the State was bound to advertise and tell the people that it wants a particular industry to be set up within the tapping contracts simpliciter there could be no objection being taken by the Government as a policy decision to the hotel group to start a Five Star hotel. [264G H] 1:3 The land allotted to the Hotel was, as we have seen, not used for the main purpose of the hotel for the establishment of a Five star Hotel, which according to the Government, was a prime need to the city of Calcutta. The land allotment to the hotels was, therefore, as it was not used in the main Zoologyogical Garden. [267A B] 1 :4 In the face of all this material, we are satisfied that the facts and circumstances brought out by the appellants do not justify an inference that the construction Of the pro posed hotel in the Begambari land would interfere in any manner with the animals in the Zo for the construc tion of a five Star Hotel, and the birds arriving at the Zira or otherwise disturb the ecology: The proposed hotel is a Garden hotel and there is perhaps every chance of the ecology and environment improving as a result of planting numerous trees all around the proposed hotel and the removal of the burial ground and dumping ground for rubbish. [268C D] 1.:5 In view Of all this, the State Government was bound by the assurance of the Chief Minister that facilities would be provided for the Zu logical Garden upon the terms set out in the two letters. The matter was taken in appeal.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to wealth tax under the Wealth Tax Act. The Income Tax Officer held that the assessee did not make valid gifts aggregating Rs. 1,50,000 on 1.1.1957 and that the gift of Rs.50,00,000 made in favour of his son was invalid. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court held that there was no valid gift on the date of the entries, then it could not be held that, subsequently, when the money was transferred by further entries in the same books, it resulted in a valid gift. In this appeal by special leave, the assessee contended that the sum of Rs 1 lakh and Rs. 50,000 could not include the gifts of Rs, 1 lakh made by the deceased to his son and to his wife respectively. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. [129E] In case there was not sufficient cash balance from out of which the amount gifted could be physically given to the donee, more entries in his accounts in the form would not constitute delivery of possession over the gifted property to the donor and gift in such cases will not be valid. The High court was in wrong in answering that question in favour. [130F] In the instant case, there was a valid transfer by debit ing the assessee 's personal account in the books of account in which the sum gifted could he physically given more entries therein in the accounts of the firm and corresponding credits to the accounts oi ties of L and K. The gift was held to be valid and as there was nothing to show that the interests which were credited in the account of the minor donees by the firm which carried on money lending business also were fictitious.

The appellant was appointed as a district judge in the Orissa High Court on October 10, 1966. He was transferred to the Orissa Administrative Tribunal by an order dated October 10 1966. The appellant challenged his transfer before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that those officers had no authority to act as law secretary, superintendent and legal remembrance and member sales tax tribunal respectively on and after October 10. 1966 and (2) commanding the State Government to send back judicial officers working in administrative posts as district judges or as addl. district judges as the case may be, after they had held those posts for three years or more. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (1) The High Courts were within its powers in posting Shri B.K. Panda as the law secretary of the Orissa high Court and the High court. [628 C] (2)(a) The rule laid down in that decision is of no assistance in determining the question as to whether the High Courts have power to fill up some of the posts in the secretariat. If this be the meaning, as the High High Court holds. then the transfer of District Judges already appointed or promoted and posted in the cadre must necessarily be outside the power of the Governor and fall to be made by the High courts as part of the control vested in it by article 235. [613 D E] (b) The order of the High 'Court posting Shri K.B. Panda was not a law secretary but an administrative remembrancer and member sale tax tribunal, respectively on or after October 12, 1966 and therefore could not be said to be vitiated. [529 G H] (3)(a). The High court was within its jurisdiction in posting the appellant as the Law Secretary, Shri B,K. Bose and Shri P.K.. But as mentioned earlier, the government had already implemented that part of that order as well. In the result these appeals are partly allowed and the order of High Court holding that Shri B was not the law Secretary, deputy law secretary and superintendent and Legal remembheat and Shri K,B.Mishra as superintendent and judicial remembraint and member Sales tax tribunal were included in the Cadre, the High Curt was within their powers in transferring Shri B to the State of Orissa. [625 G H; 627 A] (4) The transfer of a District Judge already appointed and promoted and posting in the cadres must necessarily mean that he is transferred from one post to another. If the High Judge holds that as the posts of the law clerk, deputy Law Secretary and superintendent are included in cadre, the State government or the High' Court has the power to recall them and post them as presiding officers of district courts.

The appellant, a co sharer and the respondent, a tenant in respect of certain lands, purchased land from one Smt. Ram Sarup, who held under tenancy of the vendor. The sale was challenged on the ground that it offended the fundamental right guaranteed by Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that there was no infringement of Article 19 (1)(a) of Constitution. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the suit land belonged to more than one co sharers and had not been sold jointly by all the co shares jointly, he was entitled to claim the right of pre emption under clause 'fourthly ' and 'fifthly ' of section 15(1) (b). Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The legislature desired to confer the right on certain relatives or relatives of the vendors or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section15(1), but with a view to covering all the remaining co shars not specifically mentioned the preceding clauses it used the expression 'other co shar er ' in the fourth clause which was meant to serve as a residuary clause to ensure 127 that, no co shar ters is left out. [127E F] 2. The Legislature desired to conferring the right to pre empt on specified family members of the vendee or vendors in the first three sub clauses of Section 15(i)(b) and with a further view to cover all the rest of the coowners not specifically mention the preceding words it used that the legislature desired that no co partici cation is leftout. [128E F; 128A] 3. The legislative intent was clear from the language employed in clause 'Fourthly ' in section 15 (1) of Act. It was not intended to confer a right on any relative or relatives to hold property conferred by Article 14 or 15 of the Act. [129B C] 4. The plain meaning of the expression "other cosharers" in clause "Thirdly ' is that no one sharer is left away from the vendor or vendors, who are specified in sub clauses (b) to ensure 128 that, any co shar lers is leaving out. It is not intended that a cosharer is left to be out. The words "other Co sharers" in section 2(1). refer only to those co sharmen who do not fail under clause "Fourthly". [128D E] 5. The expression 'any co sharERS ' in clause (4) of section 2 refers to only those cosharers who do either fail under clauses "Thirdally or 'Secondly ' or 'Thirdly of Section 14. [130E F]. 6. The word 'other Covers ' in cl. (4), 'fourthingly ' and the words 'otherco sharers ' in sub clause (c) to section 15 are not used in the sense that they happen to be co shared. [131G] 7. The language employed by the legislature is clear and unambiguous. It does not mean that a person who holds under tenancy or any one of them, the land or property sold or a part thereof, can claim pre emation but not the son. [132B C].

The petitioner, who was the son of one of the sons of the first respondent, filed a suit for title and injunction. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the compromise deed was not genuine and lawful and the alienees had no intention to accept the compromise. In appeal, the High Court held that once the Court was satisfied that there was a compromise it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the Court under Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the face of such a statement in the compromise Deed signed by the parties, the second respondent had disputed the fact of payment and has, therefore, no right to claim mesne profits. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the alienee that the alienation was valid and binding and the transferees have become owners of the property prior to the compromise and they even maintained that there were agreements for sale prior to 21.8.1987. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the alienations are valid and the transfers have becomeowners of the properties by the alienors. [540C] 2.1 In view of the fact that there is a allegation of payment of Rs. 1 lakh to Sudarshan Gupta which we have not investigated and to meet the further allegation that some improvements have been made to the property which too we have never gone into, it is unnecessary to refer to the facts leading to the litigation. [541D] 2:2 The alienees have admittedly been in possession of the land from the date of the sales which is more than three years old by now. In fact if the compromise is valid and enforceable the alienor respondent No. 2 had no interest in the property to part with in view of his stipulation in the agreement that on receipt of Rs, 1 lakh each and the second and third respondents have received the same. The alienee has not been able to point out any justification as to why the compromise should not be acted upon and on the basis of it the litigation may not be disposed of. [542C D] 2 :3 In view Of the fact the suit is genuine and valid, the same has to be acted on. [543D] 3:4 The alienes shall deliver vacant possession of his property by 30th April, 1991, to Seshiah and in the event of failure to do so the Trial Court is directed by our present order to deliver vacant physical possession of that property in suit including those which are covered by the sale deeds in favour of the transferees to Seshaah within one month therefrom. If necessary, the Trial court may appoint a Commissioner and take police help for executing this order and such cost shall ultimately be borne by the defaulting alienees but may initially be met by the concerned alienees and then be met from the defaulting vendees.

The workmen of the Company were granted sick leave for 7 days sick leave on full pay and dearness allowance in 1958 subject to the condition that the benefit would cease to apply when the benefits of the Employees ' State Insurance Scheme would become available to the workmen. The workmen, however felt aggrieved because of the first proviso to section 49 of the , filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the award on the ground that the Tribunal had given the benefit of sick leave and that the workmen did not deserve any relief for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the benefits admissible under the Act in the matter of grant of sick Leave are such as to justify the rejection of the workmen 's demand and the setting aside of the Tribunal 's awards in that respect. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had not given any reasons for allowing the benefit to the sick leave with retro spective effect from January 1, 1975 in view of the second proviso to Section 49 of The Act and that since the Tribunal has corrected under a mistaken impression of the sickness benefit which the Act allowed for as has been shown, it does not deal with all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit and did not, at any rate, provide for the grant of leave on Full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has committed an error in allowing the relief to the workman. [864C] 2.1 In the instant case, the Tribunal was under a misconception that 86 the sickness benefits would be lost for the second two days also. It is not necessary that in the circumstances of the case, to award the benefit, the sick Leave with retro grative effect should cease to applied when the benefit is last paid. [874D] 2:2 The Tribunal had correctly examined the matter and given adequate reasons for awarding the benefit. Such a leave could not be categorised as privilege leave as, by its very nature, it would be admissible only in the cases of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. It appears, however, that it was not necessary, in the facts of the present case to award benefit of the sick leaves with retro modtive effect on January 1 1975 in the garb of sick. [884E F] 2 :3 The Tribunal ' has cor rectly considered the controversy and given sufficient reasons for granting the benefit under 7 days Sick leave in the manner set out in the award. Such leave could be treated as privilege Leave as, By its very nomenclature, it is not a privilege leave. It was not permissible to give any reason for allowing sick leave without retro specious effect from time to time. [894G H] 2(a) The Tribunal should have given the benefits under 7 months sick leave in view Of the fact that the company had cor rected under the mistaken impression that 86 sickness benefit would be loss for the 1st two days. It has also correatedly examined whether the workmen were entitled to any of the benefits provided by the Act, and give adequate reasons therefor. Such an leave could only be categorised in the category of actual illness certified by registered medical practitioners. [904G] 2.(b) The High court was not justified in allowing a benefit of 7 days sickness leave as it would amount to granting privilege leave on half emoluments during that period of his physical incapacity.

The appellant was an Advocate of the High Court of Bombay. He had a standing of about thirty years. The grounds were not vague or not, but want of bona fides, as well as the non application of mind on the part of the detaining authority, viz., the Government which for this purpose must be taken to be different from the police. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the grounds furnished were vague and did not require any clarification. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the grounds were vague; (2) the non compliance with article 22(6) of the Constitution, and (3) the failure to furnish particulars in the affidavit related to the decision of the Advisory Board, could not be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation. HELD: (i) The order of detention was based on a consideration of the circumstances of each case as was pointed out by this Court in the State of Bombay vs Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya, ; , and (ii) that the non communication of the decision cannot be held not to have prejudiced his constitutional rights of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. [408 B C] (2)(a) The right of the detenue to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 22 (6) which includes disclosure of facts considered to be against public interest. But, the right of a detenue to have been afforded a proper opportunity of representation cannot be so exercised as to nullify the constitutional right Of representation and An obligation to supply cannot be inferred in these cases. [404 D] (b) The power not to disclose facts considered against public interests cannot be said to have impede his Constitutional right of being afforded a reasonable opportunity of making a representation. Such a contention as to the mala fide exercise of the power is untenable in the present case having regard to the nature of the activities imputed to the appellant, it will enable him to present to the Advisory board his difficulties in making a proper representation and to convey to it a request for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section 10 of the Act for their own information and consideration. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non supply of the order cannot be treated as having hampered the constitutional rights Of representation. [405 G H] (c) The failure to disclose particulars in a affidavit related with the decision taken at the time when the grounds are furnished is not fatal to the validity of the detention order. It is unnecessary, therefore, to deal in this case with a theoretical contention as regards the mala fides exercise of power is unsustainable in the light of the nature and activities imputed thereto to the petitioner. [406 G H; 407 A B] (d) The non communication by the detaining Authority cannot be construed as having prejudiced his Constitutional rights of being furnished particulars under article 19(5). It is necessary that the detenu should have been furnished with the full particulars referred to in the particular paragraph of the affidavit and there was nothing to suggest that this question was not considered by the Advisory Committee at the relevant time when it was furnished.

The respondent was a member of the Army Staff. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been convicted by a General Court Martial, and that the action taken thereunder was without authority. The Central Government directed removal from service of Capt. section K. Rao under r. 14 of the Indian Rules 1954. The Chief of the Air Staff, after going through the proceedings of the Court of Inquiry, considered that the trial of the officer by a general Court Martial was inexpedient and he ordered administrative action to be taken under r, 14 of Army Rules, 1954. On April 9, 1959, an order was passed removing the respondent from service. Rao thereupon filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from the service on grounds inter alia that r.14 of the Defence Rules, 1955, was ultra vires the , and that he should be dismissed from the services. The High Court allowed the petition holding that r 14 of Defence Rules 1954, was intra vires the . Held, that the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes it clear that there must be rules, and subject to the provision of the Act, such rules, the Central Government may dismiss or remove from the serv ice. The two sections 19 and 45 of the , are mutually exclusive. 14 Of the Army Rules 1954 is not ultra vires. It was argued that the expression "subject" occurring therein in section19 makes section 19 subject to section 45, and the Central Govern ment has thus no power to remove a person from the Service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. The words "Subject to the other provisions of the . Act and such rules , the Central Govt may dismiss, or remove" in section 21 of the read with r. 15 of the Rules are not ultra Art. 14.

The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing tea. The Company had to pay octroi duty in accordance with r. 21, and the rules relating to that tax or fee by beat of drum in the village and by means of a notice affixed in the office of the Panchayat and at the village chavdi or chora, specifying a date not earlier than one month after the date of such publication, on or after which the panchayat shall take the proposal into consideration. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of r. 22, but the High court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the rules prescribing the procedure for levying tax or fees and were not confined to octroi duty only. Held: (i) that the Standing Committee inspected the premises of the Company but in their order they have given very scanty facts, They do not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. The Standing Committee visited the premises and found that the formalities contemplated by law were complied with. (ii) that these things are done and that the resultant product was completely different from the tea imported into octroi limits. In the present case the Standing committee inspected the building of the company but in its order they had given very Scanty particulars, They did not say what the requirements of law were fulfilled. The rules prescribing procedure for imposing tax or Fee and are not confined only to octroi duties only. (iii) that it enjoins that the procedure prescribed in r. 3 should be followed before the octroi duty can be levied from the date specified in the notice and he says that if the octroi limits had not been approved of by the time the resolution was passed, how could the tax be levied therefrom.

The appellant was convicted under section 31(1) read with section 33 of the , and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 5 to a term of imprisonment for a period of six months or with fine or with both. The appellants were acquitted by the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Bombay, but the High Court reversed their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that as the conciliation proceedings had continued for a long time, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the accused persons could not be convicted under s 31(I) of the Act. Held: (i) The conciliation proceedings were pending at the time when Louis Pereira was dismissed the appellants were rightly convicted under that section. (ii) The provisions of the . , are applicable to the proceedings before a conciliation officer or a Board or of any proceeding before a Labour Court or Tribunal or National Tribunal in respect of an industrial dispute, no employer shall: (a) in regard to any matter connected with the dispute, alter to the prejudice of the workmen concerned in such dispute, the conditions of service applicable to them immediately before the commencement of such proceedings; or (b) for any misconduct connected with a dispute, discharge or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, any workmen concerned therein in such disputes, save with the express permission in writing of the authority before which the proceeding is pending. The conciliation proceeding therefore did not end when the report under section 12(6) was made by the Conciliation Officer but when that report was received by the appropriate Government. (iii) The termination of the conciliation proceeding was deemed to take place when the reference was made to a Court, Labour Court, Tribunal orNational Tribunal in the present case.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he was falsely implicated and was not at all concerned with the murder. The District Magistrate, Dhanbad in respect of the petitioner 's activities were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The petitioner made representation on 22nd January 1986 and the petitioner was informed that the said representation was rejected. On the same day, the petitioner surrendered in respect for the criminal charge against him. The grounds stated that there was indiscriminate firing on 24th December 1985 on Katras Coal Dump and the detenu started indiscriminate firing to kill Birendra Pratap Singh a rival of his calendestine business of coal to establish the criminal superiority in full view of the shopkeepers, customers and passers by of the area. In those circumstances it appears that the grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. The detaining authority rejected the representation. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The continued detention of the detenu under the Act is not justified. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power of preventive detention should not be exercised. [910C] 1.2 In the instant case, when the actual order of detention was served upon the detenu, the detenu was in jail. There is no indication that this factor or the question that the detenu might be released or that there were such a possibility of release was taken into consideration by the detaining authority properly and seriously before the service of the detention order. [ 910D] 1:3 The order of preventive Detention when it was passed was not invalid and on relevant considerations, the service could not have been exercised. In the facts and circumstances of this case, therefore, the continued detention under the act is not warranted. [936E F] 2.1 There is nothing in the petition that the detaining Authority had any reason to believe that the petitioner might be detained in custody or that he may be released on bail. The order was passed without proper consideration. It may be mentioned that in the affidavit of the District Magistrate it does not appear that either the prospect of immediate release of the prisoner or other factors which can justify the detention of a person in detention were properly considered in the light of the relevant factors. [973G] 2:2 The order is set aside. If, however, the detaining authorities are satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order of Detention was necessary for putting him back in jail, the matter of service of order was not on proper consideration by that authority properly considered by the Detaining Authority properly and critically before the Service of the Order. [978G H] 2 :3 The continued custody of the Petitioner under the , is not illegal and on irrelevant considerations, it is not proper to exercise. [977F] 2(a) In the petition it is nowhere stated that the detention was not justified and onrelevant considerations, The service of detention order was also not on improper consideration. [981C D] 3:1 The order dated 21st January 1986 passed by the District Collector, Dhanbad, in respect to the petitioner/appellant while he was in custody was not properly considered. It is nowhere mentioned that the Petitioner 's prospect of his imminent release was properly and with seriousness considered by him by the detention authority. [980D E] 2.(b) The order passed by preventive detention when it is passed was invalid and On relevant considerations the service, of the impugned order was, not on adequate consideration.

The appellant, a manufacturer of gold trade, was carrying on business as a money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business. The Administrator granted permission to carry on his business under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 for the period from 1st April, 1969 to 31st March, 1970. The appellant challenged the validity of section 28 on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred upon the Administrator could be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. The High Court struck down the aforesaid provision only on the grounds that it suffered from the infirmity of excessive exercise of legislative powers inasmuch as the Administrator had no power to refuse permission or grant permission. In these appeals by special leave, the appellant contended: (1) that section 28 confers an uncanalised and arbitrary power without anything more than any criteria or guidelines for guiding its discretion; (2) that the Administrator is given unlimited authority or power to decline permission or to grant permission; (3) that in making his orders he has regard to the policy and purpose of the Act in making its orders. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The object of putting the Act on the Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. In other words, the various restrictions that have been put on the activities of the traders doing business in gold will have to be viewed from the aforesaid perspective. [755C D] 1.2 The policy and the scheme of the impugned Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the Acts afford more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [758E F] 1:3 In the absence of parity of situation or circumstances the doctrine of parity cannot be invoked. [759D E] 1 :4. The object and scheme of section 5(1) of the , is to ensure protection of circum potances of the persons engaged in gold trade. It does not impose any blanket or 956 absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the said premises in that premises in connection with which he carries on business in as such dealer. Even the restriction in the case of a third person in carrying on his trade as a dealer but he is prevented only from carrying out business as money lender and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy, and purposes of the enactment and by the prime consideration that circumvention Of the other provision of the statute shall not be premitted. [761G H] 1.:5. The objective, the policy & the scheme affords sufficient guidance for the Administrator to exercise his discretion in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under section 5 (1). [759E F; 759A B] 2:6. While conferring power on the Administrator under section 4(1), the Administrator was required to have regard to, the anticipated demand, as estimated by him for the ornaments in that region but the expression 'anticipated demand ' was really vague and incapable of assessment leading to a great deal of uncertainty; similarly the expression (1 )AIR 1971 Patna, 240. 112.

The appellants claimed that they had acquired title by adverse possession, and the properties were not held by them as managers of the trust. The trial court found that the properties belonged to the temple and they were not holding the same as managers or trustees of the temple. In appeal, the lower appellate Court reversed the findings of the trial court and dismissed the suit. On a reference under section 66(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951, the High Court held that the property belonged to them and they had been transferred for valuable consideration. The appellants contended that the question as to whether on facts proved in this case an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removed from office by other persons who were acting as de facto managers of a Hindu endowment, was a mixed question of fact and law and the High court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below. Held: (i) The question whether on the facts proved, an inference could be drawn is not one which would govern the application of limitation but must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Where however, the transfer is made by the manager not as manager but as an individual, and he deals with the property not on the basis that it belongs to him and not to the religious endowment, the transferee is adverse from the date of the transfer. (ii) The transferor and his family had been claiming beneficial interest in the properties all along and that they were neither holding the said properties nor their own as managers. (iii)The question whether the facts established in this particular case did not show that the alienor disposed of all the property and left the village ' but also that for the last 25 years or so, the management has been taken over by other person who are acting as manager of the Temple de facto, has not been discussed by the High Courts. (iv)The High Court was in wrong in reversing this decision of the lower courts by holding that the title of the property had not been lost by adverse Possession before the suit was filed.

The appellant firm was granted a licence for exhibition of cinematographs in the cinema theatre known as Apsara Theatre. The licence was renewed by the District Magistrate in the name of Ved Gupta. On April 27, 1979, a suit was instituted against Ved Gupta and seven others by seven of the partners including Krishan Kumar for a declaration that the Cinema licence dated July 22, 1969 issued by the Sub Divisional Magistrate, Jammu (8th defendant) for exhibition thereof was the property of the firm Apsra Theatre and for a prohibitory injunction restraining defendants 1 to 7 from interfering with the running of the cinema by the plaintiffs and also for a mandatory injunction restraining them from interfering in any manner with the exhibition by the plaintiff of cinematograph films in the premises of Apsaara Theatre, Gandhi Nagar, Jammu. The District Magistrate rejected the said request by an order dated April 21, 1979. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order passed by the State Government and the Special Leave Petition by the High court was dismissed by this Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the licence granted to Ved Gupta was not the property or the partnership firm Apara Theatre; (ii) the District magistrate had no power under the Act or the Rules to make such an order; (iii) the procedure prescribed by the Act and the Rules for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the licence and answerable to the licensing authority for all commissions and omissions in the Cinema premises, was not followed by the licensing authorities before the order was passed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Licensing Authority had no jurisdiction under the provisions of the Act to suspend a licence. [578B] 2.2 In view of the fact that the licence in respect of the Apsar Theatre was granted by the competent authority in the sole name of the partnership, it could not be said that the District Judge had no powers under the Rules or to make an order. The only other reason stated by the learned Acting Chief Justice for quashing the District Magistrates ' order is that the licensing Authority had jurisdiction to suspend the licence. It was only the licensee who was held responsible under the act and rules for due observance of all the conditions of licence and liable to be punished for all acts committed by others in the capacity of licensee of the Theatre. [579C D] 2:3 The Licensing authority had no competence under the law to suspend or cancel the licence, nor could he suspend the same. [580D E] 2 :4 In view thereof, the licensing order passed against VedGupta was void and in violation of the principles of natural justice. [581E] 2(a) The High Court has rightly held that under the provision of the Jammu & Kashmir Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965, the power to suspend licence is conferred only by Section 6 F of the . It could not have exercised its jurisdiction in a writ application filed by the appellant against Ved GUPTA. [584C D; 584A] 2.(b) The licensing authority had jurisdiction under section 6 F to suspend and cancel the licences. [585D E]. 2(c) The power to grant suspension is conferred by Section6 F of . It is not an absolute power but a discretionary power. It is a discretionary one. It can be exercised only in exceptional circumstances, depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [583G H] 2 (a) In the instant case, the licence was granted to the appellant firm in the year 1977. The Licensing Authorities had no authority under the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Service (Classification Control and Appeals) Rules 1965 to make any order.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain mills and the factory in question, applied to the Custodian for cancellation of their lease granted by him under section 12 of the , but the respondent did not give any reply thereto. The Custodian issued a notice to the appellants on 13 2 1954 calling upon them to show cause why they should not be evicted. On 13 2 1951 the appellants appeared before the respondent and contended that he had no auth ority to issue the notice in question under section 10 of the . The Custodian, after considering the objections raised by the appellants, cancelled the lease granted to the appellant on the ground that the appellants had systematically committed breaches of the various terms on which the properties bad been leased to them. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the rights of the appellants in so far as they related to the purchase by them of the mills and factory were left open to the determination of the appropriate authorities, and that under the section as it now stands, the Custodian has the power to cancel leases created not merely by the evacuees but also by himself. The notice in terms refers firstly to the lease which it is proposed to cancel, and secondly to the movables in respect of which certain directions were given. In the present case, the notice was to that extent without juris,diction, and therefore the Custodian had power under section 11 to cancel the agreement to sell the mills. The notices in terms refer firstly to a lease which was in respect for property belonging to the evacuee, that there was no warrant for imposing a further limitation on that section that that lease should also have been granted by the evacuee and not by the Custodian himself, and (2) that the notice, Exhibit C, was to the extent without jurisdiction.

The appellant, a minor son of Raghubir Singh, was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March, 1963. The ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divisional Officer on 5th May, 1976 and the Board of Revenue determined the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh. On appeal by Raghubir Singh the Revenue Appellate Authority set aside the order of the SubDivisional Officer on March 6, 1973 and remanded the case to the Sub Deputy Officer, Hanumangarh, for fresh determination of the call area for grant of land for Raghubir singh. The matter was taken to the Board and by its order dated 14th April, 1975 directed that the ceiling areas for RaghubirSingh may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1955 and not according to the new law i,e.Act of 1955. In pursuance of the direction of the Board, the Sub- Divisional Officer, Bikaner held that Surendrapal Singh (appellant) aged 12 years was a minor daughter of Raghubir singh and used to 725 study in Punjab and further held that the land in possession of RaghubirSingh was ancestral. Aggrieved by the order dated May 6, 1976 passed by the Board the Sub Sub Divisional officer filed revision application before the Board for Rajasthan. The Board of revenue dismissed the same and upheld the order. The appellant preferred a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of Raghubir SINGH that no appeal having been filed by the State from the order the Sub Division Officer dated 5th April 1976, the said order became final and the board of Revenue had no jurisdiction to set aside that part of the order which had gone against the State and in his favour. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that it was not correct to say that Section 9 is limited to the executive control and superintendence of the Boards over subordinate revenue courts and it does not apply to judicial proceedings. [766C] 2.1 In the Government of India Act of 1935 there was provision under Section 224 for superintendence by the High Courts ', but subsection(2) made it clear that this superintendence would not be construed as giving to the High court any jurisdiction to question any judgment of any inferior court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. [765D] 2:2 The Board has power over all revenue courts. In view of the language of Section 221 of the Act of 1956, it is clear that the Board 's powers of superintendence and control over all Revenue Courts are similar to those conferred by Section 9 of the Land Revenue Act, 1915. [76F G] 3.1 The Board had by its orders dated 14 th April, 1976 directed that "the ceiling area may be fixed according to new law" i. e. Act No. 1 of 1955 & not according as to the old law. [77G H] 2 :3 In the instant case also the High ' Court did not go into the merits of the controversy nor did it advisable to into it and it would be for the Sub Assistant Officer, who committed the grave illegality on not merely ignoring the law but also ignored the directions of the board itself. It is clear from the language used in Section 221 that the Chairman of the State Board has general powers of supervision and control of all revenue Courts. In this case also, the High "Court" had by the impugned order dated 4th April 1975 directed the Sub Collector to decide the matter in the light of the observations of theBoard. It was not necessary for the Board to exercise its powers of judicial superintendence and it could not, therefore, make use of its powers under Section 9.

The appellant, a newspaper employee of the respondent State, was engaged in the production or distribution of newspapers and news materials. The Central Government issued an order on the basis of recommendations of Justice Palekar. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order by filing writ petition in the High Court which allowed the same holding that the law reports were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and therefore the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by it on the ground of publication of the newspaper reports was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the Law Reports were not newspaper within the ambit of section 1(b). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The law reports published by the Ist Respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the appellant in their production or publication of these public news reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the Central Government on the recommendation made by Justice P.alekar Award. [782G H] (2) The expression `newspaper ' as defined in the Act includes not merely `public news ' but also `comments on public news and information. The Act in question is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of the newspapers establishments and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of the statute the one which advances the object of the enactment and is in favour of the employee for whose benefit the Act is passed has to be accepted. [788B] (3) The word `new ' as used in section 2 (b) includes not only `public newspaper but also every other person employed to do any work in, or in relation to, any newspaper establishment. It is significant that the expression `public News ' is defined by section 2 of the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955. The definition of `new' as defined under the Act means any printed periodical work containing public news or comments on public News and includes such other class of printed periodicals as may be notified in this behalf by the State Government in the Official Gazette. [789A B] (4) The expressions `public newspapers ' and 'public news reports ' are not defined in section 1 (b). They are, therefore, matters in which the public is interested. [783C D] (5) The definition includes not mere `public publication ' but `comment on public newspaper. [784E F] (6) The words `new or periodical work ' as understood in the dictionary meaning of `public media ' and `public information ' are used in the sense that they are intended to be used for the purposes of improving their conditions of services. [779D E] (7) The term `new" is defined in Section 2(c) of Act as any working journalist, and includes any other person engaged to do or do any business in, any news establishment. [781E F]. (8) The publication of a newspaper ' as contemplated by section 1 of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, by itself may not be sufficient to make a law report a newspaper which may after some time cease to be a newspaper and become a book of reference.

The appellant was a licensee of the respondent. The agreement was described as an agreement of 'leave and licence ' entered into between the respondent on the one hand and the appellant on the other wherein the respondent had been described as the licensee and the recitals therein recite that the licensor was seized and possessed of and was otherwise well entitled as the monthly tenant of the workshop premises situated at 231, Ripon Road, Cooperative Building, Bombay. The licence was to commence from 1st September, 1965 to 31st August, 1970 and it was further submitted that the licensee had approached the licensor to allow him to occupy and use the said premises for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a period of five years and whereas the licensor had agreed to allow the licensee to use the premises under the leave and licence of the licensor for a term of five year. The respondent filed an application for eviction on the ground that he was in occupation of the premises on 1st February, 1973 under a subsisting agreement for licence. The Small Cause Court held that the appellant was not a sub tenant but a licensee and not a tenant. The High Court allowed the revision on the view that there was no subsisting agreement between the parties and that the respondent was a tenant and having found that the period of licence had come to an end, he passed an order of eviction against the appellant. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the intention of the parties in the document and the facts and circumstances of this case it is a licence and not an agreement. good deal of submission was made before us that if it was a lease and not as a lease, then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the Court had to jurisdiction, and there was nothing on record to show that after 31st March, 1966 the leave & licence agreement between parties was renewed or any fresh agreement was entered into. The appellant 's contention that it was an agreement for leave and Licence was not supported by any evidence. good dealing of submission is made before this Court that if the exclusive possession to which a person was entitled under an agreement with a landlord was coupled with an interest in the property, the agreement would be construed not as mere licence but as a licence. good dealt of submissions were made before it that if there was any error apparent on the face of the record, the error if any has to be discovered by long process of reasoning, and the High Court should not exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution. [231B C] 1.2 In view the background of the entire document evidencing the contention of the appellant that it is an agreement to leave and license, good deal o submission was submitted before this court that if this point had been taken in support of the plea that there were no subsisting contract for licence on the 1st of February 1973 as there was none on record, then the point could not be taken aid of. [232D] 1:3 In view Of the facts of this appeal and the background and the circumstances of the whole document evidencing its contention that the lease was not put an end to by the appellant and that in any event by filing the application for ejectment the appellant licensor had granted an implied licence to the respondent licensee to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour. This decision was remanded back to the High court and it is directed that the appeal be heard afresh in accordance with law because in a previous decision Vaidya, J. by the judgment dated 9th December, 1975 as mentioned hereinbefore had allowed the appellant ' s appeal.

The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Rajasthan. The Ruler of the Jodhpur State merged with the State Government and became a part of the covenanting State till such time as they were modified by the new State. On January 26, 1950, the Ruler of Jodhpur State transferred his rights to the Company under article 295(2) of the Constitution. In pursuance of this agreement the appellant company transferred its rights in favour of the Company on August 1, 1951 and on February 2, 1952, the Company was merged with it by virtue of the provisions of the Covenant. The Company continued to be a part B State of Madhya Pradesh till January 26. 1950. On March 12, 1952 the Ruler issued a notification under article 296(2), which provided that all the existing laws in the covenanted State shall continue until they were repealed or altered and the liabilities arising from the existence of those laws shall be the assets and liabilities of the Union. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the said notification on the ground that it was not in dispute that on January 26 1950, there was no recognition of the liability by the old State of Dholpur to; refund the amount of tax collected in advance for no export was made and that the liability did not devolve on the Part B State. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that article VI could not be enforced by citizens against the new sovereign as it emerged on January 1, 1950. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The agreement was not a law. It was part of an agreement between the Ruler and the Ruler. [184 D] (2) The covenant in the agreement was only a recognition of rights of subjects and that there was always recognition by the Union of India as regards the liabilities of all old States which eventually were included in it subject always to this that if the new law is within the competence of the State legislature and does not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force.

The appellants were the sellers of certain agricultural crops in the State of Madras. The appellants were not prevented from doing their business, for they could still utilise it for commodities other than the notified crops. The State Government considered them and declared the areas to be specified in the notification or any portion thereof to be a notified area for the purpose of the Act. The appellant contended that the appellants had really two fundamental rights: one was to carry on trade or business and the other was to hold their property, i.e., the market; that by reason of the notification they were not prohibited from holding the market as property, for them could still utilize it for commodity other than notified crops; and that the appellant had no right to do business in the market established subject to the regulations and also did business outside the prescribed area ; and that they were therefore not prohibited by bye laws framed under the Act, and that there was no violation of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the scheme of the bye law prohibiting the deduction of trade allowance and does not operate upon any other payments made which are not trade allowances. The object of the statute is to ensure that the market committee complies with the requirements of the law and it is not open to the Government to fix a long distance as a prohibited area; and so too, A, the seller may purport to sell one maund of cotton but in fact deduct a small part of it, retain that part for himself or give it to C. The question whether 'mahimai ' is a trade allowance depends upon the nature of that deduction. If on the other hand, mahimai ' was a deduction out of the price or commodity agreed to be paid or transferred, it would not be a deduction from the price and commodity within the meaning of section 14 of The Act.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death on the ground that they had committed a dacoity at Ramchander 's house and that they were not guilty and so should be acquitted, but the High Court confirmed their convictions. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) There was no discrepancy on the point of guilt in the case of Bhilia and Tukia because it was for that reason that they thought they must have joined in the attack and so had added that detail to their story. [457 F] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that section 377 of the Code does not abrogate or modify that provision. [404 C D] (iii) There is no evidence on record which could justify an inference of common intention in a case where two Judges concur because of section 377, but also on that of sentence. [405 G H] (iv) The fact that the appellants were acquitted by the High court was not established by the prosecution. It was not proved to have done anything except be present and even if it be accepted that Nilia aimed a blow, at Ram chander ''s thigh he did no more than inflict a comparatively light head injury. There was also evidence of enmity on the part of the accused who only joined in his attack but had no hand in the killing, and none on the side of the two who did the actual murder. There is nothing to show that any one knew who the assailants were and that therefore the accusation made against them was a subsequent concoction and that it was only for that purpose that they think they must be acquitted. [406 G H; 407 A B] (v) The evidence of Rasika and Subhana shows that there was no inconsistency on this point, but on that account it did not even hit him. [409 C D].

The petitioner was appointed as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India and was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.1976 made under Rule 56(j)(i) after he had attained the age of 50 years. The petitioner challenged that order for retirement and has claimed payment of remuneration which he would have been entitled to draw upto the normal date of superannuation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Government servant officiating in Class II service or post could be retired compulsorily by exercising the power under Rule56(j) (i) on the ground that he was not in Class 1 or Class II Service or post and had entered Government service before attaining the age Of 50 years; and that the petitioner was entitled to salary and other allowances payable to him from the date of compulsory retirement till the date he completed the age. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order for retiring the petitioner from Class I Service or Post could not be treated as a Government servant in Class 11 service or posts and that since the petitioner had attained his age of 55 years on 10.2.1972, he should be deemed to have been in Class III service or Class I services or post at the relevant time and that he would be entitled to receive salary and allowances from the dates of compulsory retire ment till the day of his normal superannuation. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The object of Fundamental Rules 56(J) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant who in Class ' I or Class ' II service Or post, whether substantively, temporarily or on officiating basis. If the officia tion is not brought to an end by reverting the Government Servant to his substantive post before the power of retirement is exercised, the Government employee con cerned must be taken to be in Class 7 or Class 11 Service or posts at the time and would come within the ambit of sub clause (i). There is, however, no warrant for the conclusion that officiating Government servants in Class 8 or Class 10 service or Post are outside the purview of sub cl.(i) of Rule 56. [638C D] 2. The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 (j)(ii) is not to confer powers on the competent authority to compulsory retire Government servants who at the first instance, have to go back to the substantive post from which he has been promoted on an officiating basis or on a tempo rary basis and it is obvious that he has no right to the post and can always be reverted to the posts, if any, on which he had a lien. [643E F] 3. The intention of Fundamental rules 56( j) is that Government servant is in Class 10 or Class III Service orpost at the same time as his substantive appointment. If he is only a temporary hand, he has to be taken into Class I or class II service and would bring within the purview Of sub clause(i). [643F G] 4. The scope of Fundamental rule 56(jj) is confined to Government servants serving in Class 9 or Class 9 service on substantive, temporary or offi ciating basis. But if he is merely a temporary employee, he can be reverted back to his original post before he attains the age o n superannuation. [538F] 5. The concept of "if he is in class I orClass II service" is not relevant to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56(q) of the Fundamental Rules. [525G H] 6. The expression "if a Government Servant belonging to a Class I and Class II services or posts is in such service orpost as covered by sub clause.(i).

The appellant Corporation had issued a cheque for Rs.2,00,000/ in favour of the respondent Corporation. The said cheque was encashed and the appellant had duly appropriated the amount and credited in the accounts towards premium payable by the deceased. In the premises it was alleged that with full knowledge of the completion of all preliminaries, the Corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards the first premium and therefore it was the case of the plaintiffs respondents that the encashment of the cheques amounted in those circumstances in law to an acceptance of the proposal. The Trial Court held that there was a concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11th January, 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant Corporation that with complete knowledge of completion of the prelim inaries, it had encashed cheques issued against the first premiums and therefore there was no concluded contract of insurance between the appellant and the respondent corporation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that there is a concluded and valid insurance contract between both the deceased as well as the Corporation, and on that basis reversing the judgment and the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge. [359E F] 2.1 In the instant case there was assurance on behalf of the field officer and local agent to the deceased that the payment of first premium would amount to acceptance of proposal if the proposal was not otherwise accepted by the Divisional Manager, on the other hand, claim was that it should be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality, if any, of sending communication of its acceptance of a proposal. [360G] 2:2 The High court was in wrong in coming into the conclusion as to the nature of the transaction between the parties and the evidence on record in this case. [361C D] 3.1 There is no presumption that the contract of Insurance is complete by offer and acceptance. It is not necessary for the plaintiff to prove that the proposer had accepted the proposal or that he was aware of it. The mere fact that the proposal sent by the proposer was for some reason does not mean that the insurer must be deemed in a position to accept the proposal unless there are cogent circumstances which indicate that the insured has accepted the offer. [362E F; 360A] 3:3 In the present case, there is no evidence that such could have been the deposition in law. The allegation that there were assurance on the part of the Field officer and Local agent to that deceased that payment would amount only to acceptance by the proposal cannot also be accepted firstly because factually it was not proved and secondly because 359 there was nothing to show that such can have been, the deposition of the witnesses in law does not create a contract of contract between either the deceased or the Corporation nor does it alter the position as under the rules the payment could never amount to the acceptance of any proposal if it was neither otherwise accepted. [363A B] 4:4 The High Courts were right in coming and holding that there had been a concluded contracts of insurance, between the appellants and the Life Insurance Corporation and on this basis reversing that judgment and decree of the Trial Court.

The appellant company was carrying on business in coal and coal. The company had been granted a certificate under section 109 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Company applied for an interim injunction restraining the company from proceeding with its business. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the order granting interim injunction did not determine the rights and obligations of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit. In appeal the High Court held that the cause of action was personal to the insolvents and did not vest in the assignee, and accordingly set aside the decree and remanded the suit for trial. The appellant company appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) An order passed by the High court in an appeal which does not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding from which appeal has arisen, is not final within the meaning of article 133(1)(c) since the controversy between the parties when the complaint in respect of offences under sections 467 and 468 read with section 114 I.P. Code was concerned merely with an order passed on by the court of the rights of the party in dispute. If the decision on an issue put an end to the suit, the order will undoubtedly be a final one but if the suit or proceedings were a live one yet to be tried, the decree is interlocutory. [934 C D] (ii) The expression "final order" in article 133 (1)(b) means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. If it did not, and the suit was still left alive and has got to be proceeded in the ordinary way no finality could attach to the order. [1034 C] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that an order by the trial court dismissing the application for interim injunction was not a final order within the ambit of article 134(1) (c) because the controversy involved between the two parties when they were the same, and it was not contended that the decision of the High Courts amounted to a judgment or decree.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk by the Panchayat Samiti in 1963 long before the Amending Act came into force on June 13, 1973. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On March 14, 1975 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On April 1, 1975, the appellant was promoted to the post of Head Clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis, Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 13 of the Amending Acts deleted section 33 of the Act. A plain consequence of this deletion was that the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. The Amending Act received the assent of the Governor 736 on April 25, 1973 and was published in the Haryana Gazette on June 12, 1973, which was published on June 14, 1973 by the Government of Haryana. Section 14(4) of the amending Act provided that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1 1973 and who were in service at the commencement of the Amendment Act shall continue to service on the same terms and conditions on which they were employed by the Panchayats Samiti, until they are absorbed in the Government service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed. Acting in pursuance of the provision of section 14(5) of Amending Act of 1973, the Government notified the absorption of the appellant as a Clerk. On May 13, 1975 the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his absorption on a lower post. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, which could not improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June 13. 1973 when the Amending Ordinance came into operation. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant was entitled to be absorbed in Government service as a teacher in any event. [775B] 2.2 The right to consider for promotion was a term & condition of Service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to claim promotion but whether the Panchayat Parishad had the right of appointment to the posts of Head Clerks on the date on which it purported to do so. Clearly, it had fortified that right on June13, 1973 when a Amending Act was brought into force. [764C D] 2:3 The Government was not bound to absorb him in the post as it purportedto do, in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed lawfully to the Post of a Head clerk and that is the post in which the Government had absorbed him. For these reasons, the High court was not right in holding that his appointment as a head Clerk was without the authority of law. [774E] 2 :4 The appellant could not have appointed the appellant on an officiating basis or in April 1975 on a regular basis. He had been appointed lawfully by the Gram Panchayat Samiti after June 12. 1973 on an Ad hoc basis and that was the post which the State had absorbed it. For those reasons, he was entitled for being considered for appointment to that post. [754E F] 2(a) The appellant is not entitled to any relief in view of section 15(4). He was appointed validly to the said post on an ex hoc basis or by April 1975. [744G H] 3:5 The right of consideration for promotion, as a term, and condition, of service were relevant for the purpose of this case.
