The appellant, a mahant of the Dera and its properties, filed a suit for possession of the properties attached to it. The defendant contended that the Dakhal at Landeke was an independent Dera, and that he was in possession of those properties as his lawful appointed mahant. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that after the death of Som Dass, Shiam Dass, as his Chela "inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a dispute is raised about such rights then the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased within the time prescribed by law. The High Court held that after Sepoy Dass died, the interest devolved upon Shiam Das as he was elected to be the Mahant of the dera. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. A suit cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest of a party in the subject matter of the suit has devolved upon another during the pendency of the litigation but that suit may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, rule 10 notwithstanding that the period of limitation for impleading them had expired. [448C D] 2. The subject matter in the suit was the interest in the Dakhra and its property and it devolved upon shiam Dass by virtue of his election as mahant subsequent to the death. [549D] 3. A person who claims (though illegally according to the appellant) as mahants of the Sepoys after the date of Septice, died during the course of the proceedings cannot be added as parties under Order 22 Rule 10 notwithstanding the fact that the limitation for impleadment had expired, and, therefore, Order 22 rule 10 will apply. [649E] 4. A devolution of interest in a subject matter may by leave of Court, be continued by oragainst the person to or upon whom such interest has come or devolved. [525C D; 526A B] 5. The suit was for possession and management of the property appertaining to it by the appellant purporting to be his de facto mahant against Som Dass as de jure mahant after the expiry of the period prescribed by Law 490 or custom that there would be devolution of any interest during the proceedings of a suit and, accordingly, Order22 rule 10 would apply. The Court said that where some of the trustees die or retire during the commencement of a proceeding and new persons are elected to fill their place, it is a case of devolution of interests during the continuance of a litigation and the elected persons can be added in as parties against them under Order22, rule10 notwithstanding that they had died. [500D] 6. The question whether the interest was in the nature of a representative character or not would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [504B C] 7. A Hindu Undivided Family is a creature of law and it has to act as an agent for the benefit of the members of the family. It is a matter of common knowledge that a person who is elected as mait by virtue o law 490 or customs can be impleaded as parties in a suit, but that does not mean that he is a representative holder of the estate of the party in whose favour the property has been acquired. [506B C]. 8. A transferee pendente lite is entitled to succeed to the property of the transferor and the transferee pendentews. The transferee pendentewani is entitled only to the share of the transferee in the transferee 's interest. [420D] 9.

The petitioners, who were Government employees in the State of Andhra Pradesh, were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Public Works Department on different dates between January 1, 1979 and October 29, 1979. The age of retirement was increased from 55 to 58 years by a notification dated October 29.8.1979. The petitioners challenged the reduction of their age of superannuation from 58 to 55. The Government of Andhra State issued a notification on September 17, 19,975 fixing the age of the employees as 55 and directing that the age should be increased from 58 years to 60. The State Government by its order dated October 16, 1979 fixed the age for retirement of all Government employees, other than in the last Grade Service, from 58 upto 58 years. The petitioner challenged the said notification on the ground that it was unreasonable. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the reduction was not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that the State Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without having regard to factors which are relevant on the fixation of the age and, therefore, the decision taken by the Government was bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of the date of retirement. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution is not violative of Article 14 or Article 16 since it is not arbitrary nor unreasonable in its circumstances. [723D] 2.1 The Government had taken a decision on its own to increase the age from 55 and 58 years, that the said recommendation was accepted by the State government and consequently, the age was raised to 58 with effect from October 29 l 979. It is not therefore arbitrary or irrational in the facts of the present case. No. The contention of the petitioners is that the proviso which conferred a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service, cannot be amended so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be changed retrospectively so as not to take away rights which had already accrued to them. [758E F] 2:2 The Government was therefore justified in its contention that arbitrary fixation of retirement age amounts to "removal" from service and is therefore violative of article 14 or 16 since the employees had acted on the representation made to them in 1979 by increasing the age Of retirement from 55 years to 58; that as a result of the increase in the age, of retirement from 58, to 55, the vested right had accrued to the petitioners, which could be taken away, if at all, only from future entrants to the Government service; and that the decision of the Government is bad for any total non Application of mind. [759E F G] 2 :3 The Government has acted unreasonably without giving any prior notice to employees who had already been stagnated in the lower positions due to expansion of educational facilities; that, the present measure was intended to have a salutary effect on the creation of incentives to the deserving employees whose number was increasing enormously due to increase in age of Retirement from 55to 58 years; that it would take welfare measures in order to improve the lot of the common man, and. particularly, in orderto afford opportunities to qualified and talented unemployed youths whose number is increasing enormally due to increased expansion of education from 55 To 58; and, the Government employees were stagnated by the increase of the ages of retirement, which was due to the increase being caused by expansion of Educational facilities; and the present action was intended for reducing the age.

The appellants are dealers in milk, and they purchased raw materials from the respondent State. The State of Haryana amended section 9(1) of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973 (for short 'the Act '). The amendment was brought into force with effect from 1st April, 1979. Section 9(2)(b) provided that where a dealer liable to pay tax under this Act, purchases goods other than those specified in Schedule B, from any source in the State and uses them in the manufacture of goods specified in Schedules B and C, from such source in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce or in the export out of the territory of India within the meaning of sub section (1) Of section 5 of the Central Sales Tax, 1956. The appellants contended that the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b) above was unduly harsh and arbitrary and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court rejected the contention on behalf of the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant State that section 9 (1)(b), which exempts only sales made in the process of export outside the territory oi ting within the State, from sales tax under section 5(3) of that Act, should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The words "or despatches the manufactured goods" used therein are not capable of being construed as including cases of despatches by a dealer of the manufactured products otherwise than through sale in his State. [351B C] 2.1 The word "dispose" used by section 9 is not susceptible of any interpretation. It is only when the goods are sold by a registered dealer and, indeed, the assessees would have had to pay sales tax on the sales made to them but for a claim for exemption under section 24. [352B C]. 2.2 The words 'disposes" used here in section 9 are not susceptible to any interpretation of the word "sale" or "purchase". It is difficult to see how the legislature intended that the expression "or dispatches" used should be construed as meaning only those sales made by a person who purchases them otherwise than for sale in that State. If the words 'or despatching the manufactured article to a place outside the State in any way otherwise than on behalf oi ser of inter state trade or business, are capable of comprehending the word 'sale ' or " purchase" it would be difficult to hold that the legislature did not intend to include those sales which were made by persons who purchased them for the purpose of export within the ambit of section 5 (3) or section 6. [353C D] 2:2 The expression "disposal" used is not capable merely because the goods were sold by registered dealers and, therefore, they could be said to have purchased them otherwise. It would be impossible to hold in a case where the manufactured articles are disposed of only by way 'pultimate sales falling under section 6 but not under section 7 or 8. [356D] 3:3 The words used therein do not mean that the goods must be sold by the registered dealer for the purposes of export. It may be pointed out that, after Act I of 1988, this provision does not tax purchases even in cases where the manufacture is exempt even if purchased by a Registered dealer for a purpose of sale within the purview of section 4 but, the goods presently in question are not laible to tax under Section 9.

The appellant was the owner of certain goods. The goods were exported by the appellant to Bombay and the goods were delivered to the sellers on their shipment. The sales tax authorities held that the goods remained the sellers ' property till they crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream, and therefore no tax was realisable on these sales in view of the provisions of article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the words " a person" in section 10(b) were not intended to be used in the sense that the property was intended to pass and did pass on the shipment of the goods. Held, that the word " a registered dealer" in article 286 (1)(a) means " a Registered dealer to whom he sells the goods". The words " only a registered dealers" are not meant to be understood in the ordinary sense of the term. It is well settled that where a person has given such certificate under section 8(b), he has the intention as stated and ultimately he sells to a person who is not a registereddealer for despatch of the consignment outside the State of Bombay, the purchasing dealer may not be liable for having made a false declaration. The words ' only a registration dealer ' are used in different senses and they are capable of being construed in their ordinary sense. In the present case the goods did not pass to the buyers on shipment but were despatched by the sellers to the appellant or by a registered registered dealer to which he sold the goods to an address outside the state of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of purchase by the dealer furnishing such certificate. The mere fact that the sales were on FOB contracts property in the goods passed to the buyer at some point of time before shipment, that is, after they had crossed the Customs barrier and therefore the sales must be held to have taken place "in the course of export" and the exemption under article 286 was not available to the purchasing dealers. The word " registered dealer ' has been defined in section 2(b)(i) as including a person whose business is carried on by him or by his agent, and includes a registered manufacturer. In order that the definition may be given in the context of the export trade, it must be shown that the person who has given the certificate under s. 8(a) is a registered trader to whom the goods have sold the articles. The fact that he sells them to a registered consumer does not make him liable for any tax. The expression " a dealer" is used in section 5(b). It means a registered or unregistered dealer to whose business the goods are entrusted and includes an agent, a registered trade association or a person engaged in the business of supplying goods. In other words, the word 'registered ' has not been defined either in the Act or in the Rules framed thereunder. The definition of "registered" is wide enough to include a person carrying on business as a dealer. It means that the expression "registered dealer" means a person registered under section 3(1) of Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947 and includes any person who carries on business in goods other than those mentioned in the Schedule. In this connection it may be said that if at the time a declaration of intention is made in the certificate the purchasing manufacturer has the knowledge as stated, and ultimately the seller sells to him a person whom he sold them but who is neither a registered owner nor a registered vendor, the certificate has not not been complied with.

The appellant, a tenant in respect of the premises leased under exhibit P 1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation of fair rent in respect thereof. The Rent Controller fixed the fair rent at Rs.994 p.m. and directed the LIC to pay the same to the appel lant within a period of two months from the date of receipt of the order. In appeal, the State contended before this Court that since the subject matter of the lease under exhibitP 1 was only a vacant site, the Rent Controller had no juris diction to fix the fair rate in respect thereto and that, therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent Control Act had to fail. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The question whether the order in the earlier proceedings is to be treated as an 570 order that is null and void or merely one that is valid until set aside, the answer has to turn on the true nature and scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the landlord under the Act. If, and only if, this relationship exists between the parties, the rent controller steps in for a limited purpose to determine what the fair rents is and then fades out of the picture. The petitioners in both the writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds. They were granted Additional licences to Export Houses/Trading Houses prior to April 1, 1988. The petitioners in these writ petitions were granted the Additional Licences under Import & Export Policy 1978 79 excluding those items which were banner in the policy for the period 1978 79 and those which have been specifically banned in the prevailing Import Policy 1985 88 pursuant to and subject to the decision of the Supreme Court dated 5.3.1986 in M/s. Rajnikant Brothers case (supra) and had imported canalised items under the said licence. The Additional Licences were valid for a period of 12 months and they contained the following endorsement: "This licence in valid for import of items permissible to Export House under the Additional Licence category as per para 176 of Import Policy 1988 79 excluding Those items which havebeen specifically banned under the prevailing import policy, 1985 88, pursuant to & subject to and the decision on the Supreme court dated 5th March, 1986 in M./s Rajnivikant Brothers, case (c) M/S. Rajkumar & Co. case (C) M.K. Jain & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors., ; , and (d) M /s. D. navinchandra & Co., case (A) M./s. J.V. Patel & Anr. vs State of Gujarat & Ors, ; , referred to. The Export Houses were granted additional licences in pursuance of the Import & Exports Policy 1978 89 and the Export Houses who were issued Additional Licences prior to that date were denied the facilities which have not been given to Export houses who were granted such Additional Licences on or after April 1 1988, on the basis of exports made during the period 1977 78. The respondents in both these writ Petitions had imported rough diamond items under a different licence and the value of licences under the Import and Export Policy 1988 91 was only 10 to 12% of the net foreign exchange earnings. The petitioner who were grant Additional Licences to the extent of 33.33% of their exports made them during the year 1977 78 cannot, therefore, be said to be persons similarly circumstanced as Export House who exported goods in the year 1987 79 and in subsequent years and obtain Additional licences for a much lesser value under the import Policy 198891 on the ground that they had imported through the same licence. In other words, under the Imports & Exports policy 1978 79 Additional licences were to be given on the strength of one third of the f.o.b. value of the exports made in 1977 78 whereas under Import and export Policy 1988 89 Additional licences are to be granted on the date of import. The appellants who were granting Additional Licences for a considerable lesser value have been denied the facility which has been given by the respondents under the Export Policy, 1978 79. In view of this Court 's order dated April 18, 1985 in Rajnanand Brothers case, the petitioners are also entitled to a similar relaxation.

The respondents were the manufacturers of excisable goods. They had been manufacturing the said goods from their factory in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer, there fore, the value had to be included in the assessable value of the excisable goods, while determining the value of such goods, the cost of packing which is of a durable nature and is returnable by it. The respondents contended that at the time of removal the goods were delivered from the factory in packing condition and containers were neither returnable nor returnable by them, there was no question of any duty being levied on the respondents. The Tribunal held that at that time of removing the goods from the factories in packed conditions, the price had tobe included in assessable value only when the packing is either manufactured by the assessee or is purchased by the manufacturer or is purchase by the assesseee. In these appeals, it was contended for the appellant that on a correct interpretation of Section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act, the Cost of packing could be included only when a packing is of durable character and returnable to the manufacturer. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The cost of such packing envisaged in section 4(3)(d) (i) does not in clude within its ambit the cost price of such pack ing which is attributable to the manufacture. [982D] 2.1 In cases where the Act provides for excise duty with reference to value of excisable articles, while determination of the value, the costs of packing, whether incurred by the manufacturers or by the supplier, has to be necessarily added to the price except where the packing consists of a packing consisting of a series of components and a number of parts. [986E] 2:2 The cost for packing envisaged under section 4 (4)(D)(i), does not include the cost incurred by manufacturer when the pack is supplied by the purchaser and recovered from the buyer except where, the packing was of duisable nature and returnable upto the manufacturer to the assessee. [987F] 2 :3 In cases wherein the Act requires excise duty to be paid with reference thereto to value, in addition to the sale price, except only where the pack ing is of goods delivered at the factory gate, an addition thereto has to been made where, in either case, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which was intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market. In this view of the matter, it is unnecessary to discuss wider questions as to the circumstances in which the cost Of packing (primary or secondary) can at all enter into the determination of its 995 assessable value under section4(4) (d)(ii). [987G H] 2.(i) The cost price envisaged in Section 4 (3)(D) does no in cluding within its purview the cost oof packing not incurred by it when the Pack is supplied at the place of removal in packed form. If this question is answered in the affirmative, then in respect of the goods so sold, thecost of such Pack ing has tobe added to price except in where the Pack consists of one or more components and an addition thereof has to he made where in addition, to the value the packing, the manufacturers levies a charged for the packings which are intrinsically or inevitably incidental thereto placing the finished goods on market.

The appellant was a private Devasthan or a public religious trust. The deity of his worship was Shri Vithal Rukhamai. The founder of the temple had already been succeeded by Guru Govindbuwa and the latter by Balkrishnabuwa, the land had been held in the year 1860 61 in the name of the Devasthan. In the absence of anything to the contrary of a convincing nature, a grant by the Government in favour of the Temple describing the property to be in charge of a manager leads to an unsupport inference that the property is a public temple. The Sanad being an ancient Royal grant was a very important piece of evidence to show that though Sakharam Maharaj, the founder of it had already succeeded by Shri Guru Govind Buwa and his heirs in perpetuity, this land had always been treated as trust property even by the Adhikari saints and the Adhikaris or the disciples who succeeded one after the other were not owners but trustees of the property. The appellant contended that the Sansthan was a public charitable trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act. Held, that when property is dedicated for the worship of a family idol, it is a private and not a public endowment. It is clear from the recitals in the document read as a whole that the dedication to the public or public user of the deity by way of grants from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of the trust, the nature of devolution of the right, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is private or a religious endowment. To sum up from the documentary and oral evidence produced, the following features are present in the present case: (1) The deity installed in the temple was intended by the Founder to be continually worshipped by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public; (2) In order to facilitate worship by the public, the Chairman also intended that regular Bhajan, Kirtan and worship shall be conducted by the saintts in succession nominated by the reigning saint.

The respondents were the trustees of the Port of Bombay. The trustees resolved that there would be a fixed recess for one hour, and that the Shore crew should work at 8 hours per week on any day. The respondent landlord filed a suit for ejectment of the appellant tenant on the ground that he was a thika tenant within the meaning of the Act as it was finally amended by an Act of 1953. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 4 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952, is prospective only, it could not apply to a case where no notice under section 4 was necessary. [742 D] (ii) The provisions of the Bengal Thika Act, 1949 as amended by the Act of 1955, are retrospective and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits, the landlord had to establish the existence of one of the grounds specified in section 3 in order to succeed. [761 C] (iii) Section 5 of the West Bengal Thiaka Tenancy ( Amendment) Ordinance 1952, does not apply where a landlord wanted to eject a thikika tenant after the Act had come into force. The provisions contained in sections 4 and 5 being prospective and assuch inapplicable to Pre Act suits. The correct view is that section 4 of Act was prospective only. [762 C] In the instant case, the question whether the respondent landlord was entitled to the benefit of the Delhi Thika tenancy (Amendment ) Ordinance, 1953, as amended subsequently by an amendment Act of 1952, could not be decided in this appeal. The appellant was working as a Bench Secretaries Grade I in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was promoted to the post of Additional Secretary Grade I on January 1, 1986. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that it would be violative of the constitutional right of equal pay for equal work. Hence this appeal by special leave. The appellant, who was the owner of the said land, had applied for mining leases in respect thereof. The respondent 's application was rejected on the ground that the appellant had waived its right to carry on business under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1956 and the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act 1961. The High Court held that the respondent was incompetent to exercise the powers of the Municipality or the Municipal Corporation had no competence to levy any tax without following the procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of the aforesaid Acts. The legislative power of the State under Entry 24 List II was eroded only to the extent to which control was assumed by the Union Government pursuant to the declaration made by Parliament in respect for a declared industry and that the field occupied by such enactment was the measure of the erosion of the legislative competence of the state legislature. The appellant was a tenant of certain lands in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The lease was for a period exceeding one year and it was not enforceable against the Government, according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the lease on the ground that the lease was not for a term exceeding one years but was for an indefinite period. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no right to terminate the lease and that as the lease had been for a fixed period, it was enforceable against him under section 20 (1) (a) of Act No. 1 of 1956. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD: (i) The words " such rights" in the third proviso are two fold namely, (a), rights created before the notified date but after July 1, 1945 for a duration not exceeding one month would be valid and enforceable by or against the State Government; and (b) that rights created after July1, 1945, are only voidable at the instance of the Government and that being the position, the Government must do some overt act to terminate such transaction. [557 B] (ii) The true meaning of the second Proviso is that rights acquired before the date of vesting are only void at the option of the State and not against the person in whose favour such right had been created by reason of section 20. [558 C D] (iii) The effect of the third provisos to sub section (1), namely, that all rights created prior to July 1 1945, for a periods exceeding one yrs would also be valid, and enforceable both by and against the government by operation of the body of sub section(1).
